articles.title: Features overview
articles.description: Everything Frameleaf can do, in one list, with links to the guides.
articles.intro: Everything you love about a big-name photo service, running on your own server. Here's a quick tour; each section links to the guide with the details.

headings.title: Your library
headings.text: Upload and view photos and videos on phone and web, with a fast, scrubbable timeline that stays smooth on very large libraries. See Library and timeline. Three layouts, grouped by day, month or year, with adjustable thumbnail size. Select and change many items at once: favourite, archive, tag, add to an album, change dates or locations. Recently added shows your newest uploads first, whatever their capture date. Hand

headings.title: Albums and organisation
headings.text: Albums and shared albums. See Albums and shared spaces. Nested albums: put albums inside folders to any depth (for example 2024, then Summer, then Beach trip), drag and drop to nest and reorder, give albums custom icons, and browse them from a tree in the sidebar with breadcrumbs on every album. Frameleaf won't let you nest an album inside its own sub-album, and warns before deleting a folder that still holds albums.

Smart search finds what's in a photo, powered by models on your own server. Search by metadata: dates, places, cameras, file names and more. articles.text: Everything you love about a big-name photo service, running on your own server. Here's a quick tour; each section links to the guide with the details. Your library Upload and view photos and videos on phone and web, with a fast, scrubbable timeline that stays smooth on very large libraries. See Library and timeline. Three layouts, grouped by day, month or year, with adjustable thumbnail size. Select and change many items at once: favourite, archive, tag, add to an album, change dates or locations. Recently added shows your newest uploads first, whatever their capture date. Handy after a big import or Google Takeout, when the files you just added have old dates. Best photos ranks your sharpest, best-exposed images using scores worked out privately on your server. It doesn't call any cloud service, create an album, copy files or change your favourites. Archive and favourites: archived items leave the timeline but still appear in search. Folder view shows your library by its folders on disk. Stacks group related shots, such as a burst or an edited version and its original, under one cover photo. Live Photos and Motion Photos back up and play back as one item. 360° photos display in the web app. Metadata view with camera details and a map for every item. Trash with a 30-day grace period by default. RAW support, with an enhanced renderer for difficult camera files. See Supported formats. Your originals are never changed. Edits to dates, descriptions, ratings and locations go to the database and an .xmp sidecar file. Albums and organisation Albums and shared albums. See Albums and shared spaces. Nested albums: put albums inside folders to any depth (for example 2024, then Summer, then Beach trip), drag and drop to nest and reorder, give albums custom icons, and browse them from a tree in the sidebar with breadcrumbs on every album. Frameleaf won't let you nest an album inside its own sub-album, and warns before deleting a folder that still holds albums. The tree and drag-and-drop live in the web app. Shared spaces for a family or group, with roles. Smart albums that fill themselves from AI-generated tags: Travel, Documents & Receipts, Screenshots, Food, Pets and Nature. They're off by default. See AI descriptions and smart albums. Tags, including nested tags and tags imported from other apps. See Tags. Storage template: choose how your originals are named and arranged on disk. See Storage template. Finding things Ask in plain words: "photos in Banff last summer", "receipts from 2024", "photos of Alice in Calgary from April 2024". See Search. Smart search finds what's in a photo, powered by models on your own server. Search by metadata: dates, places, cameras, file names and more. People and pets: face recognition and grouping that run on your server, never in the cloud. Existing face tags in your files are read in too. See People and pets. Places and map: a world map, and places by country, region and city, with names worked out on your server. See Places and map. Memories: "on this day" stories from past years. See Memories. AI descriptions All on your own server, and optional: Descriptions and tags for photos and videos, searchable like any other text. Video descriptions look at frames from across the whole clip, not just the thumbnail. Custom instructions in plain words, such as "if you see a car, identify the make and model" or "name the sport being played". Names in descriptions: people you've named are mentioned by name ("Kelly, Connor, Alexa and Jeremy at the beach"), not as "a family". Safeguards that remove names the model made up, and admin tools to review and repair descriptions and tags. There's a recommended setup order (faces, then video duplicate detection, then prompts, then names, then smart albums) that saves re-running jobs across your whole library. articles.title: First steps after installing
articles.description: Create the admin account, add the people you live with, connect your phone, choose a folder layout and protect your library.
articles.intro: After Manager setup or manual installation, open the photo application. This page takes you from an empty server to a library your whole household uses, with backups in place.

headings.title: Set up the server and create the admin account
headings.text: From a computer on your home network, open http:// :2283. Click Getting Started. A short setup opens. Your progress is saved as you go, so you can come back to it. Follow the chapters: Welcome, Account, Library, Protection and Ready.

headings.title: Try an upload
headings.text: In the web app, click Upload and choose a few photos, or drag them onto the page. They appear in your timeline straight away and are processed in the background.

headings.title: Add the people you live with
headings.text: Give each person their own account, so each has a private library, their own phone backup and their own faces and memories.

headings.title: Connect your phone
headings.text: Install Frameleaf from the App Store or Google Play. You can also use http:// :2283 in your phone's browser. See iPhone and Android apps.

headings.title: Choose a folder layout
headings.text: By default, Frameleaf names stored files with a random identifier so names never clash. The storage template gives your originals readable folders and file names instead, such as 2024/07/IMG_1234.HEIC. The layout you picked during setup is a storage template.

headings.title: Protect your library
headings.text: Frameleaf backs up its database for you every night, but it doesn't back up your photo files. You need both to restore.

headings.title: Optional next steps
headings.text: Bring in an existing photo folder without copying it: External libraries. Import from Google Photos or iCloud Photos. Speed things up with a GPU: Hardware acceleration, or run machine learning on another computer: Remote machine learning. Turn on AI descriptions and smart albums: AI descriptions. articles.text: Frameleaf Manager is the easiest way to install Frameleaf. It guides you through choosing storage, installing a verified release, setting up your account and connecting your phone. Afterwards, it gives you start, stop, logs, updates and database recovery in one place, and keeps working even when the photo application is down. On Synology, download the approved SPK and use Package Center → Manual Install. The Synology guide covers checksum verification, the package wizard, DSM HTTPS and administrator access. Native DSM setup uses your DSM administrator session; the standalone Linux claim-key steps below do not apply to it. Check Requirements before you begin. If you prefer to manage containers yourself, use Manual Docker Compose installation. Frameleaf Manager 0.2.5 is published for Linux amd64 and arm64. Its container is ghcr.io/frameleaf/frameleaf-manager:latest, which always follows the newest Manager release. The literal GitHub latest tag points to the same source commit. The release includes an Unraid template and a TrueNAS Custom App Compose file; use the Unraid or TrueNAS guide for those platforms. Manager and the photo application are separate releases. Install the photo library from the matching signed application release that Manager offers. Keep PostgreSQL 19 images and storage apart from a PostgreSQL 14 installation. Synology's native app and SPK are distributed separately; see Synology. Prepare the host Manager's launcher runs on Linux with Docker, Compose v2, Cosign, findmnt and realpath installed. Prepare four existing folders using absolute paths: Put PostgreSQL on a disk filesystem outside Docker's storage directory. Manager refuses network filesystems, RAM disks, loop-mounted disk images and Docker volumes for this location. You can choose a mounted disk in the wizard; it must already be made available to Manager. For Unraid, Manager detects Settings → Docker → Default appdata storage location and shows you the path to confirm. See Unraid. Start Manager Download launch.sh and cosign.pub from the GitHub latest tag into the same folder. These source files are separate from the release's downloadable NAS assets: Replace the example paths, HTTPS address and LAN address with your own: The launcher only accepts ghcr.io/frameleaf/frameleaf-manager:latest. It pulls the image and verifies the signature of the exact image it pulled before starting it. On Unraid, use auto instead of the appdata path to use the detected location. The final argument controls the listening address; omitting it binds Manager to 127.0.0.1. Manager uses port 2282, next to Frameleaf's 2283. Open the HTTPS address you supplied. Manager controls Docker on this host, so keep this administrative address on a trusted network. Create your Manager administrator Manager opens full screen on Secure your Manager. Manager's administrator is a separate local account. No Frameleaf Cloud account is needed. Open Manager from a device on your home network. Enter your name and a password of at least 14 characters. Select Create administrator. There's no claim key. Setup only works from your home network, and only until Manager has an administrator, so create it soon after starting Manager. This account manages the installation. You will also create or sign in to your photo library account during setup. articles.title: What is Frameleaf?
articles.description: Frameleaf is a private photo and video library that runs on your own server.
articles.intro: Frameleaf is a photo and video library you run on your own hardware: a NAS, a home server or any Linux machine with Docker. Your phones back up to it, your family shares it, and the originals stay on your disks as ordinary files.

articles.text: Frameleaf is a photo and video library you run on your own hardware: a NAS, a home server or any Linux machine with Docker. Your phones back up to it, your family shares it, and the originals stay on your disks as ordinary files. It's built for home and family libraries: Google Photos-style discovery, with faces and search worked out on your own server, and fast Cloud processing for heavy tasks whenever you approve it. Start with Frameleaf Manager for guided installation and recovery. Experienced administrators can use manual Docker Compose setup. The three parts The server, which stores your library, recognises faces, powers search and serves the web app. The open-source edition is the Frameleaf Library community edition, licensed under AGPLv3. The apps for iPhone and iPad and Android, which back up your camera roll and browse the whole library. Apple TV brings browsing, memories and slideshows to your television. The iPhone Duo guide explains the developing foldable layouts. Frameleaf Cloud, an optional plan that lets you reach your library from anywhere, keeps 1 TB of off-site backup, adds the relay for buddy backup with a friend (over a direct connection, buddy backup needs only Server licences), Sign in with Frameleaf for your family, and the Apple TV app. Cloud GPU uses wallet credit and doesn't need a plan. Your local library works fully on its own. See Frameleaf Cloud. What's inside the server A Frameleaf installation is a small group of Docker containers started from one Compose file: Your photos and videos live in one folder on the host, set by UPLOAD_LOCATION. The database lives in another, set by DB_DATA_LOCATION. What you get Everything you'd expect from a family photo service, plus a lot that's unique to Frameleaf: Backup and browsing on phone and web, with a timeline, albums, shared albums, partners and public links. Search in plain words, such as "photos of Alice in Calgary from April 2024", with faces, places and dates worked out on your server. People and pets, memories and a world map. Locked content: keep sensitive photos (medical, financial, identity documents) in your normal albums but hidden behind your PIN. AI descriptions and tags for photos and videos, written by a model on your own server, with smart albums that fill themselves. Nested albums with folders, custom icons and drag-and-drop ordering. Non-destructive editing for photos and videos, and Studio, a multitrack video editor. Library Care to find missing and damaged originals and put back verified copies. Duplicate review that keeps your HEIC or RAW original rather than a bigger re-encoded JPG, and physical deduplication so a family doesn't store the same file twice. Imports from Google Photos and iCloud Photos, and a verified server-to-server move. See the features overview for the full list. Frameleaf looks after your library carefully, but no software can stop a disk from failing. Follow a 3-2-1 backup plan: three copies, on two kinds of storage, with one off-site. See Backup and restore. Where to start Check the requirements. On Synology, install the native app through Package Center. On other hosts, install with Frameleaf Manager or follow the Unraid or TrueNAS guide. Manual options are in Other ways to install. Open the web app and work through first steps: the admin account, other people, your phone and backups. Bring in the rest of your photos from Google Photos, iCloud Photos or an existing folder with an external library. Bringing an existing collection? See Bring an existing library.

articles.text: Prefer to manage the containers yourself? This guide takes you from the release files to your first sign-in in five steps. For a guided setup with updates and recovery built in, use Frameleaf Manager. Keep the server, machine learning and database images from one matching release. Use the photo application's supplied Compose files; the separately published Manager release does not supply them. PostgreSQL 19 and PostgreSQL 14 have different physical database layouts, so keep each database directory with its own major version. Bring existing data across with the migration or restore workflow, and use the database image specified by the matching Compose file. Download docker-compose.yml and example.env from the same published Frameleaf release, and use the database image already specified in that file. These files create a new Frameleaf database. To bring in existing data, from another application or an older PostgreSQL major version, use library migration or backup and restore. Download the release files Choose a published photo application release that supplies both files, then replace below. Use the release tag rather than /releases/latest/download/, because the latest GitHub release may be a Manager component release. In a new installation folder: For a specific release, download both files from that release's asset list. For an upgrade, preserve your current .env and follow Upgrading instead. Set your storage and password Edit .env before starting anything: Replace the example storage paths and database password. FRAMELEAF_VERSION=latest selects the current application and machine learning images. Choose a long random database password containing letters and numbers, as required by the release example. The Compose file supplies the compatible database image, so your images always come from one matching release and there's no digest to copy. UPLOAD_LOCATION is the host folder containing originals and generated files. Allow room for previews, transcoded video and backups. DB_DATA_LOCATION is a new folder on local disk, preferably an SSD. Network shares are not supported for PostgreSQL. The PostgreSQL parent folder is mounted at /var/lib/postgresql. Retain the versioned database directory inside it. DB_DATABASE_NAME=frameleaf is the current example default. Preserve the configured name when restoring an existing Frameleaf installation. The release starts frameleaf_server, frameleaf_postgres and frameleaf_machine_learning. Background jobs use PostgreSQL; Redis and Valkey are not required. Configure optional settings Most settings belong in the web app after setup. See Environment variables for host settings, database connections, machine learning, setup, logging and worker controls. Compose reads .env for substitutions and passes the variables to services with an env_file entry, so a variable takes effect in each container that receives it. After changing .env, recreate containers with docker compose up -d; a restart alone doesn't reload their environment. For acceleration, the optional hwaccel.ml.yml and hwaccel.transcoding.yml release helpers supply GPU device mappings and runtime settings. Follow machine learning acceleration or video transcoding setup. The video guide also includes an inline Quick Sync option that does not need a helper download. articles.title: Other ways to install
articles.description: Install Frameleaf with Portainer, the install script, non-root containers, a NAS or a rented server.
articles.intro: On Synology, install the native Frameleaf Manager app with Package Center → Manual Install. For other supported hosts, start with Frameleaf Manager for guided installation. Use manual Docker Compose setup when you want to own the container configuration yourself.

headings.title: Portainer
headings.text: Download the release's docker-compose.yml and example.env. In Portainer, create a Stack and paste the Compose file. Replace each .env reference under env_file with stack.env. Add the release's environment variables in the stack editor. Set an absolute UPLOAD_LOCATION, a new DB_DATA_LOCATION on local disk and a random DB_PASSWORD. Set FRAMELEAF_VERSION=latest, keep the database image supplied by the Compose file, then

headings.title: Install script
headings.text: The repository's install.sh is a small helper for a fresh manual installation. It creates a new frameleaf-app folder, downloads the latest release's Compose file and environment example, generates a database password, and starts the stack. It requires Docker, Compose and curl.

headings.title: Containers running as a non-root user
headings.text: The release's docker-compose.rootless.yml runs its services as user and group 1000:1000. Use it in place of the regular Compose file. It sets the service user; your Docker daemon stays as it is.

headings.title: NAS systems
headings.text: Synology: obtain the released Frameleaf-supplied SPK and matching checksum, verify the file, then use Package Center → Manual Install on DSM 7.2.2-72806 or later with Container Manager 1432 or later. Open the app from the DSM main menu using the configured DSM HTTPS origin and create its administrator account. Library setup installs an eligible application release. See the Synology guide.

headings.title: A rented server
headings.text: A Linux VM works with the same installation guides. Give it enough storage for originals, generated files and backups. Serve the app over HTTPS, and keep the database and Manager administration private. See Reverse proxy.

headings.title: Kubernetes and all-in-one images
headings.text: Frameleaf installs with Manager or the release's Compose configuration. There's no supported Kubernetes chart or all-in-one image.

articles.text: On Synology, install the native Frameleaf Manager app with Package Center → Manual Install. For other supported hosts, start with Frameleaf Manager for guided installation. Use manual Docker Compose setup when you want to own the container configuration yourself. Manual container routes use files and images from one matching Frameleaf release. The Synology package installs Manager, which then installs the library from an eligible authenticated release. Portainer Download the release's docker-compose.yml and example.env. In Portainer, create a Stack and paste the Compose file. Replace each .env reference under env_file with stack.env. Add the release's environment variables in the stack editor. Set an absolute UPLOAD_LOCATION, a new DB_DATA_LOCATION on local disk and a random DB_PASSWORD. Set FRAMELEAF_VERSION=latest, keep the database image supplied by the Compose file, then deploy. Open the server on port 2283 and complete First steps. If your editor only accepts one Compose file, copy the hardware settings you need straight into the service. See Hardware acceleration. Install script The repository's install.sh is a small helper for a fresh manual installation. It creates a new frameleaf-app folder, downloads the latest release's Compose file and environment example, generates a database password, and starts the stack. It requires Docker, Compose and curl. Download and review the script from the release or source revision you want, then run it with Bash from a new parent directory. The script won't overwrite an existing frameleaf-app folder, which protects any library and database already there. Choose a new parent directory instead of deleting the old folder. For control over storage paths before the first start, use the manual guide instead. Containers running as a non-root user The release's docker-compose.rootless.yml runs its services as user and group 1000:1000. Use it in place of the regular Compose file. It sets the service user; your Docker daemon stays as it is. Create the library, PostgreSQL and ml-model-cache host folders before starting it, and give the chosen user the permissions each service needs. If you change the UID or GID, change it consistently in the Compose file and folder ownership. Keep the PostgreSQL parent mount at /var/lib/postgresql. NAS systems Synology: obtain the released Frameleaf-supplied SPK and matching checksum, verify the file, then use Package Center → Manual Install on DSM 7.2.2-72806 or later with Container Manager 1432 or later. Open the app from the DSM main menu using the configured DSM HTTPS origin and create its administrator account. Library setup installs an eligible application release. See the Synology guide. Unraid and TrueNAS: follow the Unraid or TrueNAS guide and use the installation files supplied for your platform and release. A rented server A Linux VM works with the same installation guides. Give it enough storage for originals, generated files and backups. Serve the app over HTTPS, and keep the database and Manager administration private. See Reverse proxy. Kubernetes and all-in-one images Frameleaf installs with Manager or the release's Compose configuration. There's no supported Kubernetes chart or all-in-one image.

articles.title: Requirements
articles.description: The hardware, operating system, storage and software Frameleaf needs.
articles.intro: Frameleaf runs happily on a modest home server or NAS. Here's what you need, and where a little extra makes it faster.

headings.title: Hardware
headings.text: Memory. Frameleaf needs at least 6 GB for a smooth experience, especially while uploads are being processed. With only 4 GB it can run with machine learning turned off, which means no face recognition or smart search. CPU. On amd64, the machine learning container needs a CPU with the x86-64-v2 microarchitecture level. Most CPUs released since about 2012 have it. In a virtual machine, choose a CPU type that passes it

headings.title: Operating system
headings.text: 64-bit Linux, such as Ubuntu or Debian, is strongly recommended. It gives the best Docker experience and is what Frameleaf is tested on.

headings.title: Storage
headings.text: Use a Unix filesystem that supports file ownership and permissions, such as EXT4, ZFS, Btrfs, XFS or APFS.

headings.title: Software
headings.text: Manual installations need Docker with the Compose plugin. Frameleaf Manager additionally requires a Linux host, Cosign, findmnt and realpath for its launcher.

articles.text: Frameleaf runs happily on a modest home server or NAS. Here's what you need, and where a little extra makes it faster. Hardware Memory. Frameleaf needs at least 6 GB for a smooth experience, especially while uploads are being processed. With only 4 GB it can run with machine learning turned off, which means no face recognition or smart search. CPU. On amd64, the machine learning container needs a CPU with the x86-64-v2 microarchitecture level. Most CPUs released since about 2012 have it. In a virtual machine, choose a CPU type that passes it through (for example host, or x86-64-v2 or newer, in Proxmox). GPU (optional). A GPU isn't required, but it makes a big difference to face recognition, smart search, AI descriptions and video on larger libraries. Intel (OpenVINO and Quick Sync), NVIDIA (CUDA and NVENC) and others are supported. See Hardware acceleration. Operating system 64-bit Linux, such as Ubuntu or Debian, is strongly recommended. It gives the best Docker experience and is what Frameleaf is tested on. Windows works with Docker Desktop or WSL 2, but expect a rougher experience and read the database notes for Windows below. macOS works with Docker Desktop for Mac. Virtual machines. Frameleaf runs well in a full virtual machine. Docker inside an LXC container isn't recommended; if you hit problems there, move to a VM. NAS systems. Synology has a native SPK installed with Package Center → Manual Install for DSM 7.2.2-72806 or later with Container Manager 1432 or later. There are separate setup guides for Unraid and TrueNAS. Storage Use a Unix filesystem that supports file ownership and permissions, such as EXT4, ZFS, Btrfs, XFS or APFS. Plan for more space than your originals take up. Thumbnails, previews, editing outputs and transcoded videos add to it, depending on your formats and settings, and processing and backups need room too. The database disk A fast, stable connection to the database matters more than anything else for a smooth Frameleaf. Put DB_DATA_LOCATION on local storage, ideally an SSD. Never use a network share (NFS, SMB/CIFS or similar) for the database. If you set Docker resource limits, give the database container at least 2 GB of memory. Corruption is most often caused by sudden power loss, network shares, SD cards or failing disks. See Check your database for corruption. Windows The database folder must be on a filesystem with Unix ownership and permissions. It won't work on NTFS or exFAT/FAT32, and it won't work under WSL on a folder mounted from Windows (usually under /mnt). For manual installations in that situation, keep the database in Linux-managed storage, such as a Docker volume. (Manager uses a supported Linux host disk rather than named database volumes.) In .env: At the bottom of docker-compose.yml: Software Manual installations need Docker with the Compose plugin. Frameleaf Manager additionally requires a Linux host, Cosign, findmnt and realpath for its launcher. On Synology, install Container Manager in Package Center, then upload the released Frameleaf Manager SPK using Manual Install. The package runs the Manager service for you, so there's no Linux launcher to run. Prepare the four storage folders and HTTPS hostname described in the Synology guide. Docker Engine is the version for Linux servers (and Windows through WSL 2). Install it from Docker's own repository rather than your distribution's packages. Docker Desktop is available for Windows and macOS. It isn't recommended on Linux. Both install the Compose plugin. You can also install it separately. Frameleaf needs the docker compose command. The older docker-compose command is deprecated and isn't supported. Ports

A DSM account in the administrators group. Frameleaf Manager appears in the DSM menu for administrators. A 64-bit amd64 or arm64 NAS that runs that Container Manager version. Allow 6 GB RAM minimum, 8 GB recommended; with 4 GB, leave local machine learni

headings.title: Prepare four folders
headings.text: In Control Panel → Shared Folder, create a dedicated frameleaf shared folder on your chosen volume. In File Station, create these four folders inside it before starting the package installer:

headings.title: Install the released SPK
headings.text: The current Synology Manager package is 0.1.0-15. Download the approved SPK and its matching SHA256SUMS from the public release. Anyone can download them; no GitHub access needed.

headings.title: Open the app and create its administrator
headings.text: Sign in to DSM as an administrator at the exact HTTPS hostname and port you entered during installation, with a DSM certificate your browser trusts. Open DSM main menu → Frameleaf Manager, or choose Open from its Package Center page. Enter your Manager administrator name and a password of at least 14 characters, then select Create administrator. headings.text: One place to start a fresh library, bring an existing Immich library or recover from a database backup.

headings.title: Open Frameleaf and connect your devices
headings.text: When the library is ready, select Open library, or open http:// :2283 from your home network using the port you chose. Create your photo library administrator and set up processing, then follow First steps to bring in your collection and connect your devices.

headings.title: Manage your library in DSM
headings.text: Service controls and logs stay close at hand. Manager remains available when the photo library is stopped.

headings.title: Protect your library
headings.text: Database checkpoints protect the library's records. Keep a separate copy of your photos and videos too.

headings.title: Update the package and the photo library
headings.text: Synology app and Manager: download the newer SPK and its checksum from Frameleaf, verify them, then use Package Center → Manual Install. The upgrade keeps your storage paths, HTTPS hostname and ports. Keep those folders available while it runs. Photo library: open Updates in the native app, choose Review update for a release, check its checkpoint and service changes, and confirm.

headings.title: Network and HTTPS
headings.text: If DSM's firewall is on, allow the DSM HTTPS port (normally 5001) from your trusted administrative network. Manager runs through that same DSM address at /frameleaf-manager/; its own connection port (normally 9443) listens only on the NAS loopback interface and stays private. Once a library is installed, allow its application port (normally 2283) from the networks your devices use. PostgreSQL needs no public port.

headings.title: Existing manual Container Manager installations
headings.text: If you run a manual Container Manager → Project deployment, keep using its release files, paths and credentials, and follow Manual Docker Compose installation and Upgrading for it.

articles.text: Frameleaf runs on TrueNAS's Docker-based Apps system. The easiest way in is Frameleaf Manager, which installs as a Custom App and then guides you through setting up, backing up and updating your library. If you prefer, you can run Frameleaf as your own custom Compose app instead. Install Manager as a Custom App Manager 0.2.5 publishes a Custom App file for TrueNAS 24.10.2.2 or later: Download frameleaf-manager.compose.yaml and SHA256SUMS, and verify the Compose file's checksum. Keep manager-manifest.json from the same release; the same SHA256SUMS covers it. Create four separate persistent folders for Manager state, library media, database backups and PostgreSQL appdata. In the YAML, replace the example HTTPS origin and folder paths with your own, keeping host and container paths identical. If you're importing a library, map its source media and database folders too. In Custom App → Install via YAML, use the edited file, then open the HTTPS address you configured and create your Manager administrator. Manager controls the host Docker engine, so keep its administrative address on a trusted network. Once it's running, Manager installs the photo application for you from a signed release. Prepare datasets Create separate datasets for the library and PostgreSQL, for example: /mnt/tank/frameleaf/library /mnt/tank/frameleaf/postgres19 Keep the live database on local storage, preferably an SSD pool. Give each dataset the permissions the release's container user needs, using the UID from that release's image. If you hit an ownership error, fix the owner rather than making the database world-writable. If your media dataset uses ACLs, let the application create and rename files and update their permissions, so the storage template works. Back up the dataset before changing ACLs on an existing library. Manual custom app Download docker-compose.yml and example.env from the same Frameleaf release. Substitute the absolute dataset paths for UPLOAD_LOCATION and DB_DATA_LOCATION. If your app editor doesn't load .env, replace each env_file entry with the environment values it needs and fill in the Compose substitutions before saving. Set a random database password. The server's DB_PASSWORD, DB_USERNAME and DB_DATABASE_NAME must match the database service's POSTGRES_PASSWORD, POSTGRES_USER and POSTGRES_DB. The new-database example uses frameleaf as its name. Use FRAMELEAF_VERSION=latest and keep the database image, dependencies, health checks and ports supplied by the Compose file. Keep the PostgreSQL parent mount at /var/lib/postgresql. Create a custom app using the resulting YAML, then inspect its container logs. From your home network, open http:// :2283 and complete First steps soon after installing. See Manual Docker Compose installation and Environment variables for the full configuration. Catalogue packages When a Frameleaf release publishes a catalogue package for your TrueNAS version, you'll find it in your catalogue, with the matching library and compatible images included. Until then, use Manager or the custom app above. Updates and backups Before updating, save a database dump, a media backup and the custom app configuration. Keep the same datasets and credentials when you apply the new release's YAML, and keep each PostgreSQL data directory with its own major-version image. Manager's Back up database protects the database and recovery configuration. Protect your photos and videos with separate backups or snapshots of the media datasets, and test a restore. See Backup and restore and Upgrading.

articles.title: Unraid
articles.description: Install Frameleaf on Unraid with Frameleaf Manager, which finds your appdata location and guides setup, backups and updates.
articles.intro: Frameleaf Manager is the easiest way to run Frameleaf on Unraid. It uses the host Docker engine, picks up your appdata location automatically, and shows you every storage and release choice before it creates anything.

headings.title: Prepare storage
headings.text: Create dedicated folders for Manager state, the library and database backups. For PostgreSQL, Manager reads Settings → Docker → Default appdata storage location. You'll see it in setup. A custom share or pool is used as you set it, and an exclusive share is resolved to its actual disk location.

headings.title: Install with Manager
headings.text: Manager 0.2.5 includes a standalone Unraid template:

headings.title: Manual Compose alternative
headings.text: If you use the Docker Compose Manager plugin, create a stack using the matching Frameleaf release's Compose file and environment example. Follow Manual Docker Compose installation.

headings.title: Native templates
headings.text: Frameleaf is listed in Community Apps. On your Unraid server, open the Apps tab, search for Frameleaf and install it. The Manager template above is also published for manual installation. A template that installs the photo application directly can need a separate PostgreSQL container on the same private network, using the exact database image and credentials the package specifies.

articles.text: Frameleaf Manager is the easiest way to run Frameleaf on Unraid. It uses the host Docker engine, picks up your appdata location automatically, and shows you every storage and release choice before it creates anything. Prepare storage Create dedicated folders for Manager state, the library and database backups. For PostgreSQL, Manager reads Settings → Docker → Default appdata storage location. You'll see it in setup. A custom share or pool is used as you set it, and an exclusive share is resolved to its actual disk location. Put PostgreSQL on a local host disk outside Docker's virtual disk and data root. Choose a new database directory, just for Frameleaf. Keep originals and database backups outside the containers. Back up the media independently; Manager's backup contains only the database and recovery configuration. Manager works with exactly the folders you give it. To use another disk, mount its folder into Manager at the same absolute host path and add it to the allowed database roots. Mount just the folders you need, not the whole host filesystem. Install with Manager Manager 0.2.5 includes a standalone Unraid template: Download frameleaf-manager.xml and SHA256SUMS, and verify the template's checksum. Keep manager-manifest.json from the same release; the same SHA256SUMS covers it. Leave Manager HTTPS origin blank and open Manager from the WebUI link, by NAS IP address or tower.local. Only if you use a custom DNS name, set Manager HTTPS origin and Advanced View → WebUI to that exact HTTPS address. Set your existing persistent folders before installing. Keep each host and container folder path identical, and update the matching advanced variables: MANAGER_DATA, MANAGER_STORAGE_ROOTS, MANAGER_DATABASE_ROOTS, MANAGER_APPDATA_ROOT and MANAGER_BACKUP_ROOT. Manager uses these paths to create sibling containers with the reviewed mappings. For an import, set Unraid autostart file to the existing unraid-autostart file in Docker's data folder, usually /var/lib/docker/unraid-autostart (check with docker info --format '{{.DockerRootDir}}'). Manager finds it once it's mounted and uses it so Immich can't start again at boot. Leave Autostart controller path blank, and leave the file field blank for a fresh install. Map any additional source media and database folders before importing. Open the WebUI from a device on your home network and follow Create your Manager administrator. The template gives Manager access to the host Docker engine, so keep its administration on a trusted network. Once it's running, Manager installs the photo application for you from a signed release. For a launcher installation instead, follow Install with Frameleaf Manager. Use auto for its appdata argument to detect Unraid's setting, or supply an explicit existing folder. In the setup review, check the database location, media mappings, application port and release. If you use a scheduler or plugin that recreates containers, pause it while an operation runs. From then on, Manager's Overview is your home for logs, database backups, start/stop and updates. Keep its exported recovery configuration somewhere private, away from the NAS. Manual Compose alternative If you use the Docker Compose Manager plugin, create a stack using the matching Frameleaf release's Compose file and environment example. Follow Manual Docker Compose installation. Set absolute host paths for UPLOAD_LOCATION and DB_DATA_LOCATION before starting, so your data doesn't land in the plugin's configuration directory on the boot device. Use a new local-disk PostgreSQL folder and the database image supplied by the Compose file. The release's named containers include frameleaf_server, frameleaf_postgres and frameleaf_machine_learning. From your home network, open the NAS address on port 2283 and set up the server soon after installing. See First steps. Already have a Frameleaf stack? Back it up, then update it in place, keeping one stack per database. See Upgrading. Native templates Frameleaf is list

articles.title: Export your library
articles.description: Download your originals with their metadata whenever you want to take your collection somewhere else.
articles.intro: Your photos are always yours. Frameleaf lets you download your untouched originals, with their metadata, whenever you like, so you're never locked in.

headings.title: Download a selection
headings.text: Select photos or videos and choose Download. For an edited item, open it and choose Download original in the viewer's More actions menu to get the untouched file; the ordinary download can include your edits. For large collections, work in batches and open a few downloads to check them. See Uploads and downloads.

headings.title: Preserve originals and metadata
headings.text: For a whole library, start with a complete backup of your library storage and database. That backup holds everything the original files don't: album membership, sharing, people and your Frameleaf settings.

headings.title: Move to another application
headings.text: Export a small sample that represents your library, including edited photos, videos and any formats that matter to you. Import the sample into the destination and compare file counts, dates, metadata and playback. Export the rest of your collection and check the result before you delete the Frameleaf copy. Keep your final Frameleaf database and media backup, so you can always recover.

Each application has its own database and folder layout, so don't point another application at Frameleaf's database or writable library folders. To move between Frameleaf servers, use Move to a new server. To recover an installation, use Backup and restore.

articles.title: Import from a folder or another app
articles.description: Bulk-import photos from folders, drives and other photo apps with the Frameleaf command line tool or an external library.
articles.intro: Photos in folders on your computer, a NAS or an external drive, or exported from another photo app, come into Frameleaf easily. Pick the way that suits you:

headings.title: Upload folders with the command line tool
headings.text: The Frameleaf command line tool, frameleaf, uploads files and folders from any computer that can reach your server. It hashes each file first and skips anything already on the server, and Frameleaf removes duplicates on its side too, so you can run it again safely. This section covers bulk uploads; for everything else the tool does, see API and CLI.

headings.title: Add an external library
headings.text: An external library leaves your files exactly where they are. Frameleaf scans the folder, adds what it finds to the owner's timeline, and scans it again every night to pick up changes. Mount the folder into the Frameleaf containers to get started. See External libraries for how to set one up.

articles.text: Photos in folders on your computer, a NAS or an external drive, or exported from another photo app, come into Frameleaf easily. Pick the way that suits you: For a Google Takeout export, use Import from Google Photos instead: it reads Google's metadata files and brings your dates, descriptions and albums along. For an iPhone or iCloud library, use Import from iCloud Photos. To move a whole library from one Frameleaf server to another, see Move to a new server. Upload folders with the command line tool The Frameleaf command line tool, frameleaf, uploads files and folders from any computer that can reach your server. It hashes each file first and skips anything already on the server, and Frameleaf removes duplicates on its side too, so you can run it again safely. This section covers bulk uploads; for everything else the tool does, see API and CLI. Install it Install the CLI by following API and CLI, using the package or container for your release. Keep its version in step with your server. The examples below use the frameleaf command on your computer. Create an API key Select your avatar in the top-right corner and choose Account settings. In Your preferences, open Account access. Under API keys, select Create API key. Give the key a name and choose the permissions the tool needs. Create the key and copy it. It's shown only once. Sign in Add /api to the end of your server address. The tool saves your credentials in auth.yml in ~/.config/frameleaf/ (or another folder you choose with -d or FRAMELEAF_CONFIG_DIR). Keep that file safe, and run frameleaf logout when you've finished. Upload Start with a dry run to see exactly what would be uploaded, without changing anything: Then upload for real. This example includes subfolders and makes an album for each folder: More examples: Upload options --delete and --delete-duplicates remove files from your computer or drive. Use them only after you've made a backup and checked the upload with a dry run. Use --visibility locked to send private photos straight into Locked. Every option can also come from an environment variable, such as FRAMELEAF_RECURSIVE, FRAMELEAF_ALBUM_NAME or FRAMELEAF_UPLOAD_CONCURRENCY. Add an external library An external library leaves your files exactly where they are. Frameleaf scans the folder, adds what it finds to the owner's timeline, and scans it again every night to pick up changes. Mount the folder into the Frameleaf containers to get started. See External libraries for how to set one up. After a big import Rejoin Live Photos. If an export split Live Photos into a separate photo and video, open Utilities, then Live Photo pairing. It matches pairs on the identifier Apple embeds in both files, and suggests lower-confidence matches on file name and capture time for you to review. See Library Care. Tidy duplicates. Imports from several sources often overlap. Duplicates helps you find them and keep the best copy. Let the background work finish. Frameleaf builds thumbnails, faces, search and descriptions after upload. Big imports take a while; follow them in Activity.

articles.title: Bring an existing library
articles.description: Find the right way to bring your existing photo server, folders of originals or online photo library into Frameleaf.
articles.intro: Wherever your photos live today, there's a straightforward way to bring them into Frameleaf. Pick the route that matches what you have, and keep your original library and a backup until you've checked everything in Frameleaf.

headings.title: Import an installation with Manager
headings.text: For a supported Immich installation, follow Switch from Immich. It walks you through Manager's review and import, shows what comes across, and explains the end of Immich backward compatibility on October 15, 2026.

headings.title: Finish and check

articles.description: Bring a Google Takeout export into Frameleaf, with dates, albums, descriptions and Locked Folder photos.
articles.intro: Leaving Google Photos doesn't mean leaving your memories' details behind. Import from Google Photos brings a Google Takeout export into your Frameleaf library, with your original files and the details Google stores alongside them:

headings.title: Get your export
headings.text: Export your Google Photos library with Google Takeout, choosing ZIP files. Download every ZIP file of the export before you start, and keep them together. Google spreads a photo's details, such as its date, place and albums, across different ZIP files. You choose them all at once, and the import matches each photo with its details even when Google put them in a different ZIP file.

headings.title: Open the import
headings.text: Open Settings, then Import & protection, then Google Photos import, and select Import from Google Photos…. You can also search for Import from Google Photos.

headings.title: Upload

headings.title: Import
headings.text: When the check finishes, the import is Ready to import. Nothing has been added to your library yet. You see what the check found:

headings.title: What happens during the import
headings.text: Each file is copied into your library. Your export files are never changed. A photo that's already in your library (the same file, by checksum) isn't copied again. It joins its albums and keeps its own date and details, unless you turned on Fill in missing details on photos you already have. headings.title: Cancel an import
headings.text: While the files upload, or once the check is done and before you import, you can select Cancel import. Select Cancel import again to confirm. It removes the import and what was uploaded for it. Photos already added to your library stay there.

This page is for the administrator; each person then connects their own Apple account by following Import from iCloud Photos. iCloud Photos Sync is off until you set it up. You need: a Frameleaf release that includes iCloud Photos Sync and its database changes, a separate HTTPS bridge container that talks to Apple, a bridge token, a private certificate and a session encryption key, a private staging folder outside every media folder, your Frameleaf web app served over HTTPS, because Apple sign-in is refused over plain HTTP. The bridge is built from the icloud-bridge folder of the Frameleaf source and added to your installation with the deployment/icloud-sync.compose.yml overlay, so you need a checkout of the source that matches your release. The bridge is based on Rclone v1.75.2, with its Go modules and container base images pinned. Choose paths and identity Add these to the environment file you use with Docker Compose, with absolute paths: Your existing media folders must already be writable by that user; the overlay doesn't change their ownership. Put the staging folder outside your upload, library, thumbnail, profile and backup folders and every external library, with no overlap. Keep it out of watched media folders and off any web server or file share. Give it to the server user with mode 0700; Frameleaf refuses a folder with wider permissions. Make sure the disk has room for the staging budgets you allow. Create the secrets Run these once on the server, for a new installation. They don't print the secret values. Never regenerate the encryption key when you update containers. Saved Apple sessions need the original key. The server expects a base64-encoded 32-byte key, not a password. Keep the CA signing key (ca.key) offline once the bridge certificate is issued. The bridge certificate lasts 365 days. Renew it before it expires. On many systems Compose secrets are bind mounts, so the ownership and permissions on the host are what count. The bridge only receives its token and TLS files. The server receives the token, the CA certificate and the encryption key. Apple passwords and verification codes are only ever typed into the HTTPS web form: never put them in .env, Compose files, command lines or support logs. Start the bridge Check the combined configuration, then start it, using your release's own Compose file: The bridge has no published port and no access to your media. It sits on its own private Docker network, which allows outgoing HTTPS to Apple. Keep it that way: no host networking and no public reverse-proxy route. The overlay sets these server variables for you: If you run separate API and worker containers, give each the same bridge and key settings and the same access to the staging folder. See Workers. articles.title: How iCloud Photos Sync works
articles.description: How iCloud Photos Sync matches, repairs and stacks your photos, keeps Live Photos and albums together, and works alongside the iPhone app.
articles.intro: iCloud Photos Sync is built to be careful with your library. This page shows what it does behind the scenes: how it recognises photos you already have, how it repairs damaged ones, and how Apple edits, Live Photos, RAW files, albums and details come across. To connect an account and run a sync, start with Import from iCloud Photos.

headings.title: Background imports
headings.text: Everything runs on your server. Once you start a sync, you can close the browser or shut your computer down; the server keeps going and picks up where it left off after a restart. A sync runs again automatically on the interval you set (24 hours by default), and you can follow it in Activity like any other background job.

headings.title: Recognising photos you already have
headings.text: The sync compares file contents, not names, so a renamed photo is still recognised and two different photos with the same name stay separate. Sometimes Frameleaf downloads a photo once to confirm it's an exact duplicate.

headings.title: Same-asset recovery
headings.text: Recovery repairs the photo you already have instead of adding a new one. The photo keeps its ID, so its albums and everything else attached to it stay in place.

headings.title: Apple edits and stacks
headings.text: With Edited versions turned on, every available Apple-edited photo or video becomes its own item in Frameleaf, grouped with its original in a stack. Open the stack to see every version and get to the original.

headings.title: Live Photo pairing
headings.text: A Live Photo is a still image, such as a JPEG or HEIC, and a short movie. The sync uses Apple's own identifiers to link the two, so they arrive as one Live Photo, with the movie as its motion part rather than a separate timeline item.

headings.title: RAW and original files
headings.text: Original files and RAW alternatives are kept as their own files. A JPEG preview is never used in place of an original HEIC or RAW file. If Frameleaf can't decode a file, it's listed for review.

headings.title: Albums
headings.text: Album names, nesting and memberships come across where Apple provides reliable information. Albums keep their identity when you rename them in Apple, and two albums with the same name stay separate. Each connection keeps its own album organisation. Photos you already had, and photos that were repaired, join their iCloud albums without being imported again. When the sync has a complete list from iCloud, it can remove

headings.title: Favourites, hidden photos and dates
headings.text: Favourites, hidden status and capture dates are kept in step where Apple's information is reliable.

headings.title: iCloud Photos Sync and the iPhone app
headings.text: The Frameleaf iPhone app can back up the same iCloud photos the sync imports. The server keeps track of which iCloud item each photo came from (its source identity), so the two never download the same photo twice.

headings.title: Counting photos and files
headings.text: A Live Photo is one photo but two files, and an edited photo or a RAW pair has extra files too. That's why the number of items settled can be higher than the number of photos you see. Imported, matched, repaired and review counts each describe a different outcome rather than parts of one total.

headings.title: Limits
headings.text: Interrupted downloads restart from the beginning of that file; a run resumes its saved work, but a single file doesn't resume part-way through. The sync doesn't delete leftover transcoded videos or XMP sidecar files.

headings.title: Not supported
headings.text: Apple Shared Albums, sharing permissions and Smart Albums. iCloud Shared Photo Library is supported. Text-message verification codes. Edited Live Photo pairing, Apple's adjustment rendering, and special slow-motion and HDR edit effects. Captions, locations and time zones from iCloud.

articles.text: iCloud Photos Sync is built to be careful with your library. This page shows what it does behind the scenes: how it recognises photos you already have, how it repairs damaged ones, and how Apple edits, Live Photos, RAW files, albums and details come across. To connect an account and run a sync, start with Import from iCloud Photos. Background imports Everything runs on your server. Once you start a sync, you can close the browser or shut your computer down; the server keeps going and picks up where it left off after a restart. A sync runs again automatically on the interval you set (24 hours by default), and you can follow it in Activity like any other background job. Each file is downloaded into a private staging folder on the server, checked, and only then added to your library. The staging budget you set for the connection limits how much space downloads in progress and recovery copies can use at once. When the budget is full, downloads wait until space frees up. Recognising photos you already have The sync compares file contents, not names, so a renamed photo is still recognised and two different photos with the same name stay separate. Sometimes Frameleaf downloads a photo once to confirm it's an exact duplicate. Same-asset recovery Recovery repairs the photo you already have instead of adding a new one. The photo keeps its ID, so its albums and everything else attached to it stay in place. The sync checks the file on disk as well as the checksum in the database. A photo imported months ago is fetched again if its Frameleaf copy later goes missing or gets damaged. Every downloaded copy passes validation before it counts as a repair. If only the movie half of a Live Photo is missing or damaged, the sync can recover just that part and leave the healthy still alone. Repairs show as Missing original restored from iCloud or Damaged original restored from iCloud in the results, and administrators can see them as resolved items in Library Care. Verified recovery copies that can't be used yet stay in staging and keep counting towards the budget. They're never deleted automatically. A validation timeout or an unsupported decoder means the file couldn't be checked, not that it's damaged. Long videos can take a while to check; your administrator can raise the time limit (see server setup). Apple edits and stacks With Edited versions turned on, every available Apple-edited photo or video becomes its own item in Frameleaf, grouped with its original in a stack. Open the stack to see every version and get to the original. For example, you crop a photo on your iPhone. In Frameleaf, the original and the cropped version sit together in one stack. Edit it again later and another version joins the stack. Which version shows. The latest Apple edit can become the one shown on your timeline, unless you've picked a different stack cover yourself or edited the photo in Frameleaf. Your choice wins, and the item is listed as Stack changed here · your stack was kept. Reverting in Apple. Reverting to the original in Photos removes the edit as the preferred version. It doesn't delete your original, older imported versions or anything you edited in Frameleaf. What's imported. Apple's finished picture or video, not its adjustment settings. You can't carry on editing Apple's sliders in Frameleaf, but you can edit the photo in Frameleaf like any other. Shared originals. Separate Apple photos with identical original files keep their own edits, even though they may share one original in Frameleaf. Version limit. Up to 20 edit versions are kept per photo. A newer version beyond that is listed for review and the existing ones are kept. Check the versions before removing any. Live Photo pairing A Live Photo is a still image, such as a JPEG or HEIC, and a short movie. The sync uses Apple's own identifiers to link the two, so they arrive as one Live Photo, with the movie as its motion part rather than a separate timeline item. If a pair is ambiguous, it's listed

articles.text: Make Frameleaf work the way you like. Your account settings cover your profile, password, Locked PIN, the features you want to see, downloads, devices and API keys, and they only ever affect your own account. To open your settings, select your avatar in the top-right corner and choose Account Settings, or open Settings from the sidebar. Settings opens on Your preferences. Use the search box at the top to jump to any setting by name. If you're an administrator, the same Settings screen also holds the server's settings. This page covers only what every account has. For the server side, see The Command Center. Where things are Your preferences App settings App settings are saved per browser or device, so you can set up each one the way you use it. Your profile Upload or remove a profile photo, and choose the avatar colour shown when there's no photo. If the server can't use a photo, your current avatar stays. Change your display name and email. A Locked photo is never used as a profile picture. Frameleaf account Link your own Frameleaf account and sign in from anywhere, even when you're away from home. You'll see this section once your administrator has linked the server to Frameleaf Cloud. Your local account keeps working too, and you can unlink at any time. Downloads & local behavior See Uploads and downloads. Features Keep your library tidy by showing only the features you use, and choose which ones appear in the sidebar. These settings change what you see, not what you have: your data stays fully available, and turning off a feature such as shared links leaves your existing links working. Your administrator can also hide a feature or turn off Chromecast for your account. If Chromecast has been turned off for you, the setting says Turned off by your administrator. Account usage statistics See how many photos and videos you have and how much space they use. Access & security Password Enter your current password, then the new one twice. Sign out my other devices is on by default; the device you're using stays signed in. If you've forgotten your password, ask your administrator to reset it. Locked folder PIN Create, change or clear the six-digit PIN that protects your Locked photos and videos. You enter it to unlock your session. Forgotten it? Choose Forgot your PIN? and enter your account password to clear it. Your locked photos stay locked. If your server has password sign-in turned off, your administrator can clear your PIN for you. Sign-in provider If your server uses a sign-in provider, such as your own identity service, connect or disconnect your account here. If your administrator has set up the provider's account page, you can open it from here too. Locked tags & people Choose which tags, people and pets stay Locked, and whether the rules cover My photos and videos or All photos and videos I can access. The rules are hidden until you unlock with your PIN, and can only be changed while you're unlocked. See Locked rules. Signed-in devices See everywhere your account is signed in. Sign out one device, or every device except the one you're using. API keys API keys let other apps and scripts, such as the command-line tool, use your account. Create a key with only the permissions an app needs, or with full access. Edit a key's name and permissions. Rotate a key to get a new value. The old value stops working straight away. Delete a key you no longer use. A new or rotated key is shown only once, so copy it somewhere safe. Notifications Email arrives once your administrator has set up the server's mail settings. See Notifications. Saving changes Change as many settings as you like, then save. If you changed your settings in another tab or on another device in the meantime, Frameleaf keeps your changes on screen and asks you to load the latest values before saving, so your work in both places is safe. Change history lists every preference you've saved, with when it was saved and the old and new values.

headings.text: An AI description added to each photo's description field, in an AI description: block. Anything you wrote yourself is kept: the generated block is added once, after your text, and never replaces it. With identity injection on, a descr

headings.title: Search with descriptions
headings.text: Descriptions make your library easier to search in three ways:

headings.title: Names in descriptions
headings.text: When identity injection is on, Frameleaf tells the model who it recognised in the photo, using the names you've given in People, and where they are in the frame. The model has to use each name at least once and mustn't fall back on words such as "a family", "a group" or "everyone".

headings.title: Videos
headings.text: Video descriptions tell the story of the whole clip. Frameleaf cuts six evenly spaced frames from each video, ranks them, and keeps them as the video's moment frames. To describe the video, it lays the frames out as one grid, in time order, and tells the model how long the video is and when each frame was taken. The model then describes the video as a whole, including what changes from frame to frame.

headings.title: Video moments
headings.text: Jump straight to the part of a video you want. A video's Moments section in the info panel shows its frames ranked best first, the cover frame and its timestamped moments. Choose a frame or moment to play from there.

headings.title: When results go out of date
headings.text: Each generated result remembers what it was made from, so Frameleaf refreshes only what needs it:

headings.title: Edit or remove a description
headings.text: The description is an ordinary field: open a photo's info panel and edit it as you like.

headings.title: Smart albums
headings.text: Tags from descriptions feed six ready-made albums: Travel, Documents & Receipts, Screenshots, Food, Pets and Nature. They fill themselves as descriptions finish, and anything you take out stays out. See Built-in smart albums.

headings.title: Privacy
headings.text: Descriptions are made by your own server's machine learning container, or by a computer on your home network that your administrator has added. Your photos only go to Frameleaf Cloud if your administrator routes descriptions there and records consent. Locked photos are described like any other, but their descriptions and tags only appear in your unlocked session. Tags are visible to anyone you share a photo with. To

headings.text: Descriptions are set up in Settings, then Search & intelligence, then Descriptions & tags. The full guide is Set up AI descriptions.

articles.text: Find any photo by describing it. Frameleaf writes plain-sentence descriptions of your photos and videos and tags what's in them, all on your own server. Descriptions name the people you've recognised, make your library searchable by what's actually in each shot, and feed smart albums that gather your travel, food and pet photos for you. Your administrator turns descriptions on and chooses how they're written. See Set up AI descriptions. Generated descriptions and tags are an early, alpha-quality feature. They already make search better, and they'll keep improving. What you get An AI description added to each photo's description field, in an AI description: block. Anything you wrote yourself is kept: the generated block is added once, after your text, and never replaces it. Searchable tags for visible objects, scenes, text and context, all lowercase and without duplicates. They're ordinary tags, so you can browse and filter by them. Names, not "a family". With identity injection on, a description says "Kelly and Connor playing baseball" instead of "a family playing baseball". Video descriptions that cover the whole clip, not just its first frame. For example, a photo of a car might be described as "A red Tesla Model 3 parked in a driveway at dusk", with tags such as car, driveway and dusk. Search with descriptions Descriptions make your library easier to search in three ways: Smart search gives a boost to photos whose description matches your words. The Description search mode finds words in descriptions, yours and generated ones. Tags from descriptions work with the tag: filter and the Tags filter. See Search and Search syntax. Names in descriptions When identity injection is on, Frameleaf tells the model who it recognised in the photo, using the names you've given in People, and where they are in the frame. The model has to use each name at least once and mustn't fall back on words such as "a family", "a group" or "everyone". Frameleaf then checks the result: Only your names are used. Any other name the model writes is replaced with "Someone". Days, months, holidays and well-known places, such as "Monday", "December", "Christmas" or "Paris", are allowed. One person, named. If one known person is in the photo and the model writes "the woman" or "the boy", Frameleaf puts the name in. Several people. If several known people are in the photo and the model uses a general word, Frameleaf leaves the sentence as written, since the word could mean any of them. Frameleaf passes only named people who aren't hidden. Faces that were detected but not named are skipped. Keeping names up to date Descriptions keep up with your corrections. Fix a face or a name in People, and descriptions that used the old name are redone the next time descriptions are processed. Naming someone new applies to descriptions written from then on; your administrator can redo older ones. See "Someone" where you expected a name? That person isn't named on that photo yet. Add them in the photo's People list and ask your administrator to rerun the description, or edit the description yourself. Videos Video descriptions tell the story of the whole clip. Frameleaf cuts six evenly spaced frames from each video, ranks them, and keeps them as the video's moment frames. To describe the video, it lays the frames out as one grid, in time order, and tells the model how long the video is and when each frame was taken. The model then describes the video as a whole, including what changes from frame to frame. A video description might read: "A short clip of Connor swinging a bat in a backyard; he begins facing the camera, swings the bat to his right, and walks off-frame at the end." The faces Frameleaf found in the video's thumbnail are used to name the people in it. A video that's shorter than a fraction of a second, longer than three hours, or can't be read gets no description. Its status shows skipped with the reason video-frames-unavailable. articles.title: Set up AI descriptions
articles.description: For administrators, how to choose a model, tune the prompt, name people in descriptions and describe an existing library without redoing the work.
articles.intro: Give everyone on your server searchable descriptions that name the people in their photos. This guide is for administrators: it shows you how to turn on AI descriptions, pick the right model, tune the prompt and describe your existing library in one pass. You'll find the settings in Settings, then Search & intelligence, then Search & recognition, then Image descriptions and tags.

headings.title: Before you start
headings.text: Your machine learning container is working, ideally with hardware acceleration. See Hardware acceleration. The model you pick is a Qwen2.5-VL or Phi-3.5-vision model, not Florence-2. For names in descriptions, facial recognition is on and you've named some people. See People. Videos need nothing extra. Each video's moment frames are cut the first time it's described.

headings.text: Already started in a different order? No problem. You can re-queue at any time, and re-evaluate smart albums one album at a time.

headings.title: Quick setup

Make sure Write captions for photos is on. Choose a Caption model. The default, Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct, suits most servers. Make sure Mention people I have named is on. Select Save changes. headings.text: List settings take one entry per line.

headings.title: Custom instructions
headings.text: Custom instructions is the easiest way to change how the model writes without touching the whole prompt. Treat it like a short brief to a careful assistant: write full sentences, say what to do and when not to, and keep it to a couple of paragraphs. The text is added to the prompt before the output rules, so the model reads it first.

headings.title: Identity injection
headings.text: Lower Max names to 1 or 2 for crowd photos where only the main people matter. Raise it to 10 to 15 for teams, weddings and other big groups. If a photo has more named people than Max names, some are left out.

headings.title: Raw prompt editor
headings.text: The structured settings above build the prompt for you, with safe defaults, and cover most needs. Reach for the Advanced raw prompt editor when you want something they can't express, such as a different output format or sections in another order.

You'll find the settings in Settings, then Search & intelligence, then Search & recognition, then Image descriptions and tags. Describing a whole library takes hours or days. Follow the setup order below and you'll only need to describe everything once. Before you start Your machine learning container is working, ideally with hardware acceleration. See Hardware acceleration. The model you pick is a Qwen2.5-VL or Phi-3.5-vision model, not Florence-2. For names in descriptions, facial recognition is on and you've named some people. See People. Videos need nothing extra. Each video's moment frames are cut the first time it's described. Setup order Already started in a different order? No problem. You can re-queue at any time, and re-evaluate smart albums one album at a time. Quick setup Go to Settings, then Search & intelligence, then Descriptions & tags. Set Kind of graphics card to match your server: auto-detect, Intel iGPU (OpenVINO) or NVIDIA GPU (CUDA). Make sure Write captions for photos is on. Choose a Caption model. The default, Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct, suits most servers. Make sure Mention people I have named is on. Select Save changes. Use Try it on a few photos to check the result on a few of your photos and videos. Under Caption progress, choose Update captions now, check the estimate, and confirm. Turn on smart albums if you want them. New uploads are described automatically after their thumbnails are made, using your current settings. Choose a model The Description model list shows an estimate of the video memory each model needs: Custom… lets you type any Hugging Face model ID from the Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL, Phi-3 and Phi-3.5-vision, and Florence-2 families. Models from other families fail with Failed to load model in the worker logs. A model downloads the first time a job uses it, which takes a few minutes. Only the Qwen and Phi models follow the prompt and your own instructions. Florence-2 writes short captions, tags and text and doesn't use your own instructions, vocabulary, indicators or identity injection. The model list describes it as "Short captions, tags and text; not for long descriptions." Each model comes with its own licence. Check the licence for the model and revision you download. See Model licences. Fallback model The Fallback model keeps descriptions flowing when the main model can't run. Florence-2 is the usual choice because it's small enough to share a GPU with other models. If the main model fails on a local machine learning server, Frameleaf retries the same request with the fallback. Frameleaf Cloud always uses its chosen model, so it doesn't need a fallback. Hardware On Intel, use the OpenVINO machine learning image and leave the description device on AUTO, which picks the best device and falls back when the GPU isn't available. On NVIDIA, use the CUDA image and choose NVIDIA GPU (CUDA). Description models download from huggingface.co unless you set HF_ENDPOINT to your own mirror. See Where models come from. Your photos are processed by your own machine learning container, and Frameleaf sends no telemetry. articles.title: Albums and shared spaces
articles.description: Organise photos into albums and collections, pin what you use often, and share a whole library with a family or group in a shared space.
articles.intro: Bring order to your library your way. An album holds photos and videos. A collection groups albums on one shelf, and nested albums let you build a tree of albums inside albums. A shared space gives a family, a trip or an event one shared library, while everyone keeps ownership of their own photos.

headings.title: The Albums page
headings.text: Open Albums from the sidebar to see everything in one place: a shelf for each collection, then your albums that aren't in a collection, then your shared spaces.

headings.title: Albums
headings.text: To add photos, select them in your library and choose Add to album, or open an album and add from there.

headings.title: Pinned items
headings.text: Pin up to 50 things you open often: albums, smart albums, saved searches, people, pets, memories, and built-in views such as Favourites, Videos and Locked. Pins appear in the sidebar and sync across your devices.

headings.title: Shared spaces
headings.text: A shared space is a library a group builds together, such as "Family" or "Iceland 2026". Everyone sees the whole story in one place, and everyone who adds a photo stays its owner.

headings.title: Privacy
headings.text: Locked items never appear in a shared album or space, whoever's looking. Edited versions follow the privacy of their original straight away.
