With Reduce Motion on, photos show without the slow drift. Play from your iPhone Pick something on your iPhone and watch it on the TV: Open Frameleaf on the Apple TV. Make sure both devices are on the same network and signed in to the same Frameleaf account. On an album, person, memory or search page in the iPhone app, choose Play on Apple TV, then the TV's name. If you don't see the button, check that the TV app is open, both devices are on the same network, and local-network access is allowed. This plays through the Frameleaf TV app; see Casting for Google Cast and other ways to watch. Top Shelf, Siri and SharePlay Top Shelf previews show On this day, memories and favourites right on the Home screen. Selecting a preview opens its page; Play starts it. Siri phrases include “Play photos in Frameleaf”, “Show photos in Frameleaf” and “

articles.title: iPhone and iPad
articles.description: Connect to your server, back up your camera roll, free up space and edit photos with the Frameleaf app for iPhone and iPad.
articles.intro: Frameleaf for iPhone and iPad backs up your camera roll to your own server, checks every photo arrived safely, and puts your whole library at your fingertips, at home or away. It's a native app with a built-in editor, widgets, Siri and Live Activities.

headings.title: What you need
headings.text: An iPhone or iPad on iOS or iPadOS 26 or later. The background upload feature described below needs 26.1. A Frameleaf server you can sign in to. For Frameleaf Cloud services: a server linked to Frameleaf Cloud. You can also use your own remote access connection.

headings.title: Get started
headings.text: When you open the app you can:

headings.title: Browse your library
headings.text: Library shows everything in one edge-to-edge grid, newest first. Pinch to change the size, or switch between Years, Months and All. The header shows the day and place you're looking at. Times are shown in the photo's own local time. A photo taken at 6:42 in Banff reads 6:42 wherever you are. Press and hold a photo for a preview with Favourite, Share, Add to Album, Save to iPhone, Hide and Delete. Select several photo

headings.title: Back up your photos
headings.text: Open Backup from the account sheet. Two thin rings show how safe your phone is:

headings.title: Free up space
headings.text: Free Up Space removes photos and videos from your iPhone once your server holds an identical copy, checked by SHA-256. You see a summary first, then confirm Remove from iPhone.

headings.title: Edit photos and videos
headings.text: Tap Edit in the viewer. Edits never change your original: your server keeps each saved edit as a new version of the same photo, and you can always go back. See Editing.

headings.title: Outside the app
headings.text: Widgets

headings.title: App lock and Locked items
headings.text: Turn on Require Face ID in Settings, then App Lock. Frameleaf asks for Face ID (or Touch ID, Optic ID or your passcode) when it opens and each time you come back. While it's locked, the app switcher shows no photos, and backup keeps running.

headings.title: Offline
headings.text: The app keeps a copy of each server's library catalogue on the phone, so dates, places and search keep working without a connection. Settings, then Storage shows how much space the offline library and the thumbnails use, and can clear the thumbnails and previews. The offline library is removed when you remove the server from the phone.

headings.title: Notifications
headings.text: Your server can tell you when backup needs you, when something's shared with you, or when a video is ready. Notifications are encrypted by your server so that only your phone can read them. Turn each kind on or off per server in Settings, then Notifications:

headings.title: Settings
headings.text: You: profile picture and name, password and PIN (with Sign Out Other Devices), signed-in devices, linked accounts, API keys (the secret is shown once), and every account preference on the server. This iPhone: Backup, Notifications, App Lock, Storage and Connection. Server: connection details, whether this phone backs up there, and a storage chart. About: the licence and Terms of Use, and Rate Frameleaf on the App Sto

headings.title: Privacy
headings.text: Your photos stay private. Frameleaf never sends photo content, search text, server addresses, filenames or Frameleaf account identifiers to Google Analytics, and advertising features and advertising and vendor identifiers are turned off.

headings.title: Frameleaf Cloud in the app
headings.text: The server owner can see Frameleaf Cloud plans right from Backup. The purchase screen shows the storage allowance, price, renewal, sharing and cancellation terms, and purchases through the App Store use its billing controls.

headings.title: Coming later
headings.text: These aren't in the iPhone app yet: viewing Locked items, signing in to servers that only use their own OAuth provider, and deleting your Frameleaf account from the app. Studio is already here on iPad, and iPhone Duo and wide windows covers the sidebar and fold-aware layouts.

headings.title: Moving from another photo app
headings.text: Switching is easy:

articles.text: Frameleaf for iPhone and iPad backs up your camera roll to your own server, checks every photo arrived safely, and puts your whole library at your fingertips, at home or away. It's a native app with a built-in editor, widgets, Siri and Live Activities. Install Frameleaf from the App Store on iPhone or iPad, then connect it to your server. What you need An iPhone or iPad on iOS or iPadOS 26 or later. The background upload feature described below needs 26.1. A Frameleaf server you can sign in to. For Frameleaf Cloud services: a server linked to Frameleaf Cloud. You can also use your own remote access connection. The app is dark only for now, and one app covers both iPhone and iPad. Get started When you open the app you can: Sign in with Frameleaf. This opens your Frameleaf account sign-in in a browser sheet. The servers linked to your account, ones you own and ones shared with you, appear on their own, and the app signs in to each without a second password. Use a server on this Wi-Fi. The app looks for Frameleaf servers on your network. iOS asks once for permission to find devices on your local network; the app explains why first. Enter a server address, then your email and password for that server. If your server signs people in only through its own OAuth provider, the iPhone app can't sign in to it yet. Use the server's website for now. The discovery card When a server is found on your Wi-Fi, or listed in your Frameleaf account, a card slides up showing its name, your role and "Online · on this Wi-Fi". Choose Connect, Not Now or Don't offer again. If there are several servers, they page inside the same card. The card appears at most once per launch and never interrupts the editor, a purchase or a permission prompt. After you connect, it asks whether to back up this iPhone to that server. Set up a brand-new server from your phone On your home network you can claim a server that has no administrator yet. There's no setup code. Setup only works on the same Wi-Fi as the server, and only until it has an administrator, so set a new server up soon after installing it. Choose Set up on the discovery card. Give the server a name. Choose Link to Your Frameleaf Account and sign in with Frameleaf. You become the owner and don't need a server password. On a server with Frameleaf Cloud, the app always uses Sign in with Frameleaf and doesn't offer a password. If you'd rather use a password administrator there, for example without a Frameleaf account, create it on the server's first-run web page instead. On a server without Frameleaf Cloud, the app creates a local administrator with your email, name and password. That account works on its own, and you can reach it over a VPN or your own HTTPS server address. Optional Cloud services each have their own short setup, which you can do whenever you like. A server that's already linked A server on your Wi-Fi that's already linked to a Frameleaf account is never set up or linked again. Its card shows Frameleaf server with Sign in, and the welcome screen offers Use “ ” on this Wi-Fi. Sign in with Frameleaf to join it, or choose Connect if it's already in your account. If the server has no administrator yet, the first sign-in of the account that owns it creates the administrator. Several servers Every server on the phone is listed with your role (Owner, Admin or User) and how the app is reaching it: The app picks the fastest route on its own and switches back to Home when it can. Tap a server to switch to it. To stop using the relay from this phone, turn off Use the Frameleaf Relay in Settings, then Connection. Sign out removes this phone's copy of that server's library, its caches and its upload queue. Nothing is deleted from the server. Servers behind a proxy Most people never need this. A server at home, Frameleaf Cloud remote access and the Frameleaf relay all connect without it. It's only for a server you've put behind your own reverse proxy or access gateway that asks for extra headers or a clie

articles.title: iPhone Duo and wide windows
articles.description: Fold-aware library layouts, windows, drag and drop and Frame mode for iPhone Duo and iPad.
articles.intro: Frameleaf makes the most of iPhone Duo. It fits itself to the outer display, the inner display and the fold, so your photos always look their best however you hold the phone. Wide windows on iPad get the same roomier layouts.

headings.title: Closed and open
headings.text: On the outer display, you get the familiar iPhone tab bar and photo grid. Open in New Window lives in wider windows, so you won't see it here.

headings.title: Around the fold
headings.text: Book pose: the grid leaves room between columns for the fold. Compare puts one item on each side, and the grid/photo divider follows the fold. Propped pose: the viewer and editor put the photo above the fold and controls below it. Frame: the photo stays above the fold while its controls sit below.

headings.title: More than one window
headings.text: Keep two parts of your library open side by side:

headings.title: Drag and drop
headings.text: Select photos and drag them onto an album in another Frameleaf window to add them. The other window refreshes that album straight away. Drag a photo to another app to share its original file.

headings.title: Use Frame
headings.text: Frame turns any album, person or memory into a living photo frame:

headings.title: If a control is missing
headings.text: Open in New Window needs a regular-width window. Photo beside the grid needs a Library window wide enough to fit both. Fold-aware layouts appear when the device reports its pose. If it doesn't, you get the normal iPhone layout.

articles.text: Frameleaf makes the most of iPhone Duo. It fits itself to the outer display, the inner display and the fold, so your photos always look their best however you hold the phone. Wide windows on iPad get the same roomier layouts. The Duo layouts are part of the iPhone and iPad app. Install Frameleaf from the App Store and follow iPhone and iPad to connect your server and set up backup. Closed and open On the outer display, you get the familiar iPhone tab bar and photo grid. Open in New Window lives in wider windows, so you won't see it here. On the inner display, open the sidebar from its toggle. On iPad, a wide window opens with the sidebar already showing. Make the Library window wide enough and the photo appears right beside the grid; narrow or rotate it and you're back to one at a time. Either way, the app keeps your place in the grid. Around the fold Book pose: the grid leaves room between columns for the fold. Compare puts one item on each side, and the grid/photo divider follows the fold. Propped pose: the viewer and editor put the photo above the fold and controls below it. Frame: the photo stays above the fold while its controls sit below. These layouts follow the fold position your device reports. They use the same library and backup you already have, so there's nothing extra to set up. More than one window Keep two parts of your library open side by side: In a regular-width window, open the menu on an album, person or memory. Choose Open in New Window. Each window keeps its own navigation and open photo. App Lock covers every window when the whole app leaves the foreground. Send one window away while you keep using another, and the active one stays open. Account sheets and incoming links open in a single window, not in all of them. Drag and drop Select photos and drag them onto an album in another Frameleaf window to add them. The other window refreshes that album straight away. Drag a photo to another app to share its original file. Drop photos from Files or another app into Frameleaf to upload them to the selected server. Drop them onto an album to upload them and add them there in one step. Progress and any failures show in the usual backup screens. For privacy, a drag started before a lock, sign-out or server switch stops exporting that library's photos. Use Frame Frame turns any album, person or memory into a living photo frame: Open an album, person or memory page. Choose Frame. It shuffles the selection and changes photos every ten seconds. Tap to show controls. Pause or leave when you're done. While the device is charging, the screen stays awake. On battery, normal auto-lock applies. Leaving the app pauses playback, and changing account or server closes Frame. When App Lock kicks in, it covers the slideshow too, so your photos stay private. If a control is missing Open in New Window needs a regular-width window. Photo beside the grid needs a Library window wide enough to fit both. Fold-aware layouts appear when the device reports its pose. If it doesn't, you get the normal iPhone layout.

articles.title: Audio and music
articles.description: Set levels, fades, panning and EQ in Studio, add a music bed or a voice-over, and keep every source channel in the export.
articles.intro: Good sound makes a film. Studio keeps your camera sound, music and voice on separate tracks, so you can balance them until everything sits just right.

headings.title: Clip sound
headings.text: For each clip you can set:

headings.title: Track and master sound
headings.text: Each track has a fader, pan and its own EQ, and can be muted or soloed. The master controls the whole mix's level and mute, separately from your computer's volume. Ducking lowers the music while a voice-over plays.

headings.title: Music
headings.text: Add a music file from your library as a music bed on the music track.

headings.title: Voice-over
headings.text: Record a voice-over with your microphone, or generate one from text, and Studio places it on the voice track.

headings.title: Tidy up speech
headings.text: Studio finds silences and filler words such as "um" and offers to remove them. You review every suggestion before anything changes.

headings.title: Sound in the export
headings.text: Choose one of the channel layouts your render worker offers: keep the source channels, or mix down to stereo. A short sample is the quickest way to hear the result. See Exporting.

articles.title: Captions and voice-over
articles.description: Transcribe speech into editable captions and generate a voice-over from text, on your own hardware or on Cloud GPU.
articles.intro: Studio turns the speech in your video into captions, and turns your text into a voice-over. Both land on the timeline ready to edit, so your films are easier to follow and quicker to narrate.

headings.title: Captions
headings.text: Transcribe listens to a sequence and turns speech into timed captions on the timeline. The result is ordinary caption text you can edit.

headings.title: Voice-over
headings.text: Type a script and Studio reads it aloud, placing the result on the voice track.

articles.text: Studio turns the speech in your video into captions, and turns your text into a voice-over. Both land on the timeline ready to edit, so your films are easier to follow and quicker to narrate. Captions Transcribe listens to a sequence and turns speech into timed captions on the timeline. The result is ordinary caption text you can edit. Transcription runs: On your own hardware, using speech models that run locally. On Cloud GPU, after you confirm an estimate. Only the sound is sent, never the picture. The job dialog shows the model, languages and limits. Speaker labels aren't available yet. Captions in the export Pick the caption style that suits your output: burned into the picture, a sidecar subtitle file, or an embedded track where the format supports it. Export a short sample to check timing, text and appearance before you render the full project. Voice-over Type a script and Studio reads it aloud, placing the result on the voice track. On your own hardware, several voices are included. On Cloud GPU, choose from the voices shown in the job dialog, which also lists the limits and how your text is handled. You can also record your own voice-over with a microphone. See Audio and music.

articles.title: Colour
articles.description: Grade clips in Studio with exposure, contrast and saturation, colour wheels, curves, LUTs and scopes, in SDR or HDR projects.
articles.intro: Give every clip the look you want, from a quick exposure fix to a full grade. Studio has the tools colourists use, with scopes to keep you accurate and automatic HDR handling for phone footage.

headings.title: Quick adjustments
headings.text: Select a clip and open the colour controls to change its exposure, contrast, saturation and temperature. Reset grade puts a clip back as it was.

headings.title: Colour wheels and scopes
headings.text: In Advanced mode you get:

headings.title: More colour tools
headings.text: The editor also includes:

headings.title: HDR projects
headings.text: A project becomes an HDR project automatically when it contains HDR media, such as HDR video from a phone. There's no switch to set.

articles.text: Give every clip the look you want, from a quick exposure fix to a full grade. Studio has the tools colourists use, with scopes to keep you accurate and automatic HDR handling for phone footage. Quick adjustments Select a clip and open the colour controls to change its exposure, contrast, saturation and temperature. Reset grade puts a clip back as it was. Colour wheels and scopes In Advanced mode you get: Colour wheels for Lift, Gamma and Gain, each with its own reset. They work with the keyboard too. Scopes: a luma waveform, a vectorscope and an RGB histogram, each labelled with its colour space. In an HDR project, use them as a guide while you grade; the browser preview isn't an HDR measurement. More colour tools The editor also includes: Levels and curves, for the whole image or for red, green and blue separately Hue, vibrance, temperature and tint A secondary qualifier to pick a colour range, such as skin or sky, and correct only that Power windows, an ellipse or rectangle that limits a correction to part of the frame Gradient maps LUTs: apply a .cube file with an intensity control Black and white, sepia and invert The colours on your screen are an approximation. For critical work, check the result on a calibrated display. HDR projects A project becomes an HDR project automatically when it contains HDR media, such as HDR video from a phone. There's no switch to set. The project keeps your HDR footage's intent all the way to export. To export in HDR, use a render worker that can keep HDR colour. On a standard display, an HDR project's preview is tone-mapped rather than clipped, and labelled Tone-mapped preview, not the colour reference. See Exporting for the HDR formats you can export.

articles.title: Exporting
articles.description: Export a Studio project on your tablet, your server or a render worker at home, in formats up to 4K, HDR10 and ProRes.
articles.intro: Turn your project into a finished film at up to 4K, in HDR, with every source audio channel. Exports from browser Studio render on your Frameleaf server or a render worker on your home network, so the render stays at home. Tablet apps can also export right on the device, or hand the render to a server worker. Studio's final render doesn't use Cloud GPU.

articles.title: Restoration
articles.description: Remove noise and compression from old videos, rebuild detail, and add smooth motion, with a preview first and the original always kept.
articles.intro: Bring old, small or damaged videos back to life. Restoration cleans up noise and compression, rebuilds detail and can add smooth motion. Open the Restore panel from the photo viewer or from Studio. Every restoration is saved as a new version, so your original file is never changed.

headings.title: Choose a mode
headings.text: Then choose:

headings.title: Choose where it runs
headings.text: You pick the destination, and nothing is processed until you do. Each destination tells you whether your video stays on your network or leaves your network for this job.

headings.title: Preview first
headings.text: Choose a small area: the current frame, or a crop. The preview is 5 seconds long. Compare before and after with a split divider and a 100% loupe. Choose Accept to restore the whole file at full resolution with the same settings, or reject it and try again.

headings.title: Use the restored version
headings.text: A restored video appears as a version of the original. You can:

articles.text: Bring old, small or damaged videos back to life. Restoration cleans up noise and compression, rebuilds detail and can add smooth motion. Open the Restore panel from the photo viewer or from Studio. Every restoration is saved as a new version, so your original file is never changed. Restoration runs on a restoration worker on your network or on Cloud GPU. Choose a mode Then choose: Size: same size or larger, up to 4K (3840 × 2160). Cloud GPU restores at up to 2×. Keep film grain to preserve fine grain instead of smoothing it. Choose where it runs You pick the destination, and nothing is processed until you do. articles.title: Database storage and recovery
articles.description: Where Frameleaf keeps its PostgreSQL database, how to store it well, and how to back it up, restore it and fix connection problems.
articles.intro: Frameleaf keeps everything it knows about your library in PostgreSQL: accounts, albums, media records, settings, search indexes and background job state. Your photo and video files stay in library storage. Back up both, and you can bring your whole library back.

headings.title: Use the database supplied with your release
headings.text: Frameleaf runs on its own PostgreSQL 19 image with pgvector, already set in the current Compose file. Use that image as it is; you don't need to enter an image digest. Keep it rather than a generic PostgreSQL image, and keep the PostgreSQL major version that created an existing database directory.

headings.title: Choose storage
headings.text: Put the database on a local disk, ideally an SSD, with room for the database, temporary migration space and backups. Keep the live database off NFS and SMB shares.

headings.title: Connection settings
headings.text: The release uses database:5432 inside the private Compose network, so PostgreSQL stays private and isn't published to your LAN. The application receives DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD and DB_DATABASE_NAME; Compose passes those values to PostgreSQL under its POSTGRES_* names.

headings.title: Backup and restore
headings.text: Backup and restore has the full procedure. To move a database between machines, use a logical backup rather than copying a live PostgreSQL directory.

headings.title: Diagnose connection failures
headings.text: For manual installations:

Your photo and video files stay in library storage. Back up both, and you can bring your whole library back. Use the Compose file and database image that come together with your release. PostgreSQL 19 and PostgreSQL 14 use different physical database layouts, so move an existing database directory between them only through the supported migration or restore workflow. It checks the location for you and won't use Docker's data root, Docker volumes, loop-mounted images or memory-backed filesystems. Manual installations: DB_DATA_LOCATION names the host folder. The release mounts it at /var/lib/postgresql; keep the versioned directory inside it. The example uses ./postgres19, relative to the Compose project folder. Connection settings The release uses database:5432 inside the private Compose network, so PostgreSQL stays private and isn't published to your LAN. The application receives DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD and DB_DATABASE_NAME; Compose passes those values to PostgreSQL under its POSTGRES_* names. To use your own database, configure DB_HOSTNAME, DB_PORT and credentials, or DB_URL, which overrides the separate connection values. It needs the same PostgreSQL version and extensions as the release. See Environment variables. Changing a connection setting points Frameleaf at a different database; it doesn't copy or migrate your data. Backup and restore Backup and restore has the full procedure. To move a database between machines, use a logical backup rather than copying a live PostgreSQL directory. Save a database backup and a matching media backup. Preserve the installation configuration and any encryption or recovery keys. Restore into a fresh destination using the matching Frameleaf release. Check sign-in, albums, a few originals and background processing, then retire the old installation. Coming from another photo application? Import its library into a fresh Frameleaf database rather than attaching its database directory. See Bring an existing library. Most connection failures come down to disk space, a missing mount or the wrong database path, so check those first. Keep any failed database directory as it is until you have a verified recovery copy.

articles.title: Environment variables
articles.description: Every environment variable Frameleaf reads, for storage, the database, Frameleaf Cloud, machine learning and more.
articles.intro: Most Frameleaf settings live in the web app. The few that shape the installation itself, such as where your files live and how the database connects, are environment variables, usually in the .env file next to your docker-compose.yml. This page lists them all; feature guides cover a few more. If you use Manager, make lifecycle and storage changes there instead.

headings.title: The basics
headings.text: These are used by docker-compose.yml itself and don't reach the containers directly.

headings.title: General
headings.text: To choose where your photos are stored, set UPLOAD_LOCATION, not FRAMELEAF_MEDIA_LOCATION. The second is the path inside the container, so a host folder there won't work.

headings.title: Database
headings.text: DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD and DB_DATABASE_NAME are passed to the database container as POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_PASSWORD and POSTGRES_DB. New installations use the database name frameleaf; an existing Frameleaf database keeps the name it was set up with.

headings.title: Frameleaf Cloud
headings.text: Create a link token in your Frameleaf account under Servers, then Add server. It works once and expires within an hour. Remove it from .env once the server shows as linked. A malformed token, port or network stops the server at startup. See Frameleaf Cloud account.

headings.title: Library Care
headings.text: Each entry is an absolute path inside the container, optionally labelled. A copy found there is copied into library storage before the item is relinked to it.

headings.title: App releases
headings.text: These let your server offer its own signed builds of the Frameleaf apps.

headings.title: Help links
headings.text: Help, settings and sign-in pages only show these links when they're set. A value that isn't an HTTPS address, or that contains a user name or password, stops the server at startup.

headings.title: Workers
headings.text: See Workers and where jobs run.

headings.title: Stopping
headings.text: Both must be positive, and the grace period must end before the deadline, or the server won't start. Docker kills the container when its stop timeout ends, so stop_grace_period in docker-compose.yml must be longer than the deadline. The supplied Compose files and NAS packages use 10 seconds, which fits the defaults.

headings.title: Machine learning
headings.text: These server variables set the starting machine learning settings. Once settings are saved, change them in the web app.

headings.title: Keep secrets in files
headings.text: DB_HOSTNAME, DB_DATABASE_NAME, DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD, DB_URL can be read from files instead, using Docker secrets or systemd credentials. Either:

headings.title: No telemetry
headings.text: Frameleaf has no telemetry metrics listener, and older telemetry options don't turn one on. For health checks and logs, see Monitoring.

headings.title: Existing variable names
headings.text: Use the FRAMELEAF_ names above. Supported older names still work, and startup tells you the new name to switch to. If both names of a setting are set to different values, the server won't start, so keep one value under the current name. To bring a library from another application, import it rather than reusing its database.

articles.text: Most Frameleaf settings live in the web app. The few that shape the installation itself, such as where your files live and how the database connects, are environment variables, usually in the .env file next to your docker-compose.yml. This page lists them all; feature guides cover a few more. If you use Manager, make lifecycle and storage changes there instead. After changing .env, recreate the containers with docker compose up -d. A plain restart doesn't pick up the new values. If a change still doesn't show, run docker compose up -d --force-recreate. In the tables, Containers says which container reads the variable: the server, the machine learning container or the database. If you split the server into separate api and microservices workers, give each the variables it needs. The basics These are used by docker-compose.yml itself and don't reach the containers directly. Use the version and service definitions that come with the release, and keep its internal Compose service names. The containers you'll see are frameleaf_server, frameleaf_machine_learning and frameleaf_postgres. General To choose where your photos are stored, set UPLOAD_LOCATION, not FRAMELEAF_MEDIA_LOCATION. The second is the path inside the container, so a host folder there won't work. If you turn on the built-in security headers (FRAMELEAF_HELMET_FILE=true), they tell browsers to upgrade every request to HTTPS, which breaks a server reached over plain HTTP. Use your own helmet file with "upgrade-insecure-requests": null if you can't use HTTPS. Ports Database DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD and DB_DATABASE_NAME are passed to the database container as POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_PASSWORD and POSTGRES_DB. New installations use the database name frameleaf; an existing Frameleaf database keeps the name it was set up with. DB_URL looks like postgresql://user:password@host:port/database. Use the SSL mode your database requires, with certificate verification for a remote database. When DB_URL is set, DB_HOSTNAME, DB_PORT, DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD and DB_DATABASE_NAME are ignored. Give the database settings to every server worker. Background queues live in PostgreSQL too, so there's no Redis or Valkey to run. Frameleaf Cloud If the identity key is lost, the server gets a new identity, and every link and licence tied to the old one stops working until you link and activate again. A copy found there is copied into library storage before the item is relinked to it. App releases These let your server offer its own signed builds of the Frameleaf apps. The folder must contain app-arm64-v8a-release.apk, app-armeabi-v7a-release.apk, app-x86_64-release.apk and app-release.apk. Android downloads and Obtainium setup are only offered when all three Android variables are set, and a value that's set but invalid stops the server at startup. Include {version} in the folder so Obtainium recognises each new release. Help links Help, settings and sign-in pages only show these links when they're set. A value that isn't an HTTPS address, or that contains a user name or password, stops the server at startup. Workers See Workers and where jobs run. The supplied Compose files and NAS packages use 10 seconds, which fits the defaults. Machine learning These server variables set the starting machine learning settings. articles.intro: Already have years of photos in folders? An external library brings them into Frameleaf without copying or moving a single file. Frameleaf scans a folder, such as an existing archive on your NAS, and adds what it finds to the owner's timeline. The files stay where they are, and they look and behave like any other photo: they appear on the map, go in albums, and so on.

articles.text: Already have years of photos in folders? An external library brings them into Frameleaf without copying or moving a single file. Frameleaf scans a folder, such as an existing archive on your NAS, and adds what it finds to the owner's timeline. The files stay where they are, and they look and behave like any other photo: they appear on the map, go in albums, and so on. Managing external libraries needs an administrator account. Each library belongs to one person, chosen when you create it. Mount the folder Frameleaf runs in Docker, so first make the folder visible inside the container. In docker-compose.yml, add a line under volumes: in the frameleaf-server service: The part before the colon is the folder on your computer; the part after is where the container sees it. The :ro at the end makes the folder read-only to Frameleaf. Remove it only if you want Frameleaf to be able to delete files there or write XMP sidecar files next to them. Then run docker compose up -d. If you run separate worker containers, mount the same folders there too. Create the library Select Settings in the sidebar to open the Command Center, then open Libraries. Select Add external library. Enter a Library name and choose the Owner. Ownership is fixed after the library is created. Under Import folders, select Add folder and enter the folder as the container sees it, for example /mnt/media/old-pics, not /home/user/old-pics. Optionally add Exclusion patterns (see below). Select Create library. Saving doesn't start a scan. Select the library in the list, then select Scan library. Each folder is checked as you add it. Frameleaf tells you if it doesn't exist, can't be read, is a file rather than a folder, is inside Frameleaf's own upload folder, is inside another import folder of the same library, or is already imported by another library. Use absolute paths. To check that it's working, open Settings, then Computers & background work, then Background work. You should see Library scans, Making thumbnails and Reading photo details at work. The library's own page shows the scan's progress, and you can Cancel scan. A library can have up to 128 import folders and 128 exclusion patterns. Folders are scanned including subfolders, and a file in more than one folder is only added once. Example: two libraries Say you want to add childhood photos, a Christmas trip whose Raw subfolder holds camera RAW files you don't want, and videos from the same trip. Create a library called "Christmas Trip" with the import folder /mnt/media/christmas-trip and the exclusion pattern **/Raw/**, then scan it. Create a second library called "Old videos and photos" with the import folders /mnt/media/old-pics and /mnt/media/videos, then scan it. You could put all three folders in one library, as long as nothing in the other folders matches the Raw exclusion. Leave files out By default every file in the import folders is added. To skip some, add exclusion patterns. They match the full file path: * matches within one file or folder name, and ** matches any number of subfolders. Escape special characters such as @ with a backslash. Simple patterns like these work best. Saving new folders or exclusions stops a scan that's in progress. Scan again afterwards. Keep the library up to date Frameleaf doesn't see changes to an external folder until it scans it again. Nightly scan. Every library is scanned once a day, at midnight by default. This also finishes removing any library whose removal was interrupted. Change the schedule. Open Settings, then Libraries, then External Library. Under Periodic Scanning, keep Enable periodic library scanning on and choose one of the Cron expression presets, or enter your own Cron expression, for example 0 0 * * * for every night at midnight. Scan everything now. In Libraries, select the button that scans them all, for example Scan 3 libraries. Library watching [EXPERIMENTAL] imports new and changed files as soon as the operating system reports them, without a resca

articles.title: Jobs and queues
articles.description: How Frameleaf processes your library in the background, what each job queue does, nightly tasks, concurrency, and splitting the server into separate containers.
articles.intro: Almost everything Frameleaf does with a new photo or video happens in the background as jobs: reading its details, making thumbnails, finding faces, indexing it for search, transcoding videos and more. Jobs wait in queues, and the server works through them as fast as its settings allow.

headings.title: Concurrency
headings.text: Concurrency is how many jobs of a kind each server worker runs at once. Raise it to clear a backlog sooner; higher values share CPU, GPU memory and disk bandwidth, and machine learning jobs use more video memory.

headings.text: The frameleaf_server container runs several workers:

articles.title: Maintenance mode
articles.description: Pause your Frameleaf server for everyone while you restore a backup or work on its storage, and sign back in if you get locked out.
articles.intro: Maintenance mode gives you a quiet server to work on. It takes your server offline for everyone else while you do administrative work, such as restoring a database backup or replacing a library disk, and shows them the maintenance page instead.

headings.title: Start maintenance mode
headings.text: Go to Settings, then Maintenance, then Maintenance mode. Under Maintenance mode, optionally type a Reason shown on the maintenance page, such as "Replacing the library disk". A preview shows what people will see. Choose Start maintenance and confirm.

headings.title: End maintenance mode
headings.text: Sign in on the maintenance page as an administrator and end it there, or run:

headings.title: Signing in during maintenance
headings.text: Maintenance mode uses its own sign-in, and Frameleaf handles it for you: if you start it from Settings, you're signed in to the maintenance page automatically when the server comes back.

articles.text: Maintenance mode gives you a quiet server to work on. It takes your server offline for everyone else while you do administrative work, such as restoring a database backup or replacing a library disk, and shows them the maintenance page instead. While it's on: Everyone else sees the maintenance page instead of their library and is signed out. Administrators sign in on the maintenance page to end maintenance or restore a backup. Uploads, mobile backups and shared links pause until maintenance mode ends. Frameleaf turns maintenance mode on by itself when you restore a database backup, and the server stays in it until you end it. Start maintenance mode Go to Settings, then Maintenance, then Maintenance mode. Under Maintenance mode, optionally type a Reason shown on the maintenance page, such as "Replacing the library disk". A preview shows what people will see. Choose Start maintenance and confirm. You can also start it from the command line, from your Compose folder: The command prints a sign-in address for the maintenance page: End maintenance mode Sign in on the maintenance page as an administrator and end it there, or run: Signing in during maintenance Maintenance mode uses its own sign-in, and Frameleaf handles it for you: if you start it from Settings, you're signed in to the maintenance page automatically when the server comes back. If you're ever signed out, any of these gets you back in: Look in the server logs (docker logs frameleaf_server) for the maintenance mode message followed by a sign-in address. The address uses your Public server URL (Settings, then Frameleaf Cloud, then Remote access) or, on a linked server, the address Frameleaf Cloud published. If the server has neither, it prints only the path (/maintenance?token=…); open that path on the address you normally use to reach Frameleaf. Run enable-maintenance-mode again. While maintenance mode is on, it issues a new sign-in address. Or run disable-maintenance-mode, sign in normally, and start maintenance again from Settings, then Maintenance. See Server commands for how to run commands.

articles.title: Recover missing or damaged media
articles.description: Find moved originals, put back verified copies and understand missing, damaged and orphan reports in Library Care.
articles.intro: When Frameleaf can no longer read an original, Library Care finds it again or puts back a verified, byte-for-byte copy, and the photo keeps its albums, people and links. This page is the administrator's side: what to check first, how recovery picks a safe copy, and what each count and report means.

headings.title: Start with storage access
headings.text: A missing-file report means Frameleaf can't reach the file it expects. Usually the file is still there: a moved or offline drive, a changed mount path and wrong permissions all look the same.

headings.title: Find a file that moved or was renamed
headings.text: In Library Care, open Missing media and run a scan. Choose Locate originals and, in Choose candidate originals, pick where to look: library storage, external libraries and any recovery locations. Review each candidate. It shows whether it's an exact match and whether it opens correctly. Choose Relink verified matches, then open the item to check it.

headings.title: Recover a matching copy from iCloud
headings.text: If the same original is still in iCloud, iCloud Photos sync brings back a verified copy.

headings.title: Understand the results
headings.text: Trash confirmed damage moves recently re-checked damaged items to the trash after a PIN and typed confirmation. Use it once you've given up on recovering them: iCloud sync doesn't restore items you trashed on purpose.

headings.title: Why the counts differ
headings.text: Different screens count different things, so compare the same scope and filters before you conclude anything is lost.

headings.title: Orphaned transcodes and XMP files
headings.text: Treat an orphan report as a list to investigate, not a deletion list. A transcode has different bytes from the original video, and an XMP sidecar is a separate metadata file, so neither matches the original's checksum. The iCloud connector leaves orphans alone and doesn't reconnect transcodes or sidecars.

articles.text: When Frameleaf can no longer read an original, Library Care finds it again or puts back a verified, byte-for-byte copy, and the photo keeps its albums, people and links. This page is the administrator's side: what to check first, how recovery picks a safe copy, and what each count and report means. The tools are in Library Care: Missing media and Damaged media. They're administrator tools; you can review your own findings, one other account or all accounts. Another person's Locked items are never listed, counted or changed. Start with storage access A missing-file report means Frameleaf can't reach the file it expects. Usually the file is still there: a moved or offline drive, a changed mount path and wrong permissions all look the same. If many files go missing at once, check your mounts and permissions first. Restoring access is often all you need, and every finding clears on the next scan. Keep your backups and recovery copies until you've opened the recovered media and checked it. Find a file that moved or was renamed In Library Care, open Missing media and run a scan. Choose Locate originals and, in Choose candidate originals, pick where to look: library storage, external libraries and any recovery locations. Review each candidate. It shows whether it's an exact match and whether it opens correctly. Choose Relink verified matches, then open the item to check it. Locate matches on the content checksum Frameleaf saved for the original, not on names or folders. So if a storage move renamed IMG_1234.JPG and put it in dated folders, Locate still recognises it, because the bytes are identical. Anything less certain, such as a matching name or a similar thumbnail, stays for you to review. Locate searches the configured locations, with limits on how much it scans. If it finds nothing, the file is outside those locations, or the item has no saved content checksum to match against. Items from external libraries that were checksummed from their path, not their contents, can't be matched this way. Recovery locations Recovery locations are extra folders Library Care searches for copies, such as a backup drive. Set them with FRAMELEAF_RECOVERY_ROOTS in .env, as Label=path entries separated by ; (the label is optional): Each path must be an absolute path inside the server container. The filesystem root and repeated paths are refused, and the server won't start until you fix them, so a typo is caught straight away. Mount these folders into the server container read-only. Frameleaf only ever reads them: a copy found there is copied into your library storage. Recover a matching copy from iCloud If the same original is still in iCloud, iCloud Photos sync brings back a verified copy. Turn on iCloud sync for the server, then have the person connect their Apple account. Select a library or album that contains the original, save the settings and choose Run now. The server downloads what it needs, computes content checksums and validates the media file itself. When the copy checks out, the existing item is repaired in place. It keeps its ID, albums, people and other links, and the matching findings are marked resolved without another full scan. Check the progress, then use Recent verified results, then View media to open it. The downloaded file must match the saved content exactly, so you get back your original, not a lookalike. A re-encoded, resized or edited version has different bytes and isn't used to replace it. A valid Apple-edited version can be kept as a separate member of a stack instead. If only the movie part of a Live Photo is damaged, it can be recovered on its own. Each original, edit and movie is repaired separately. Managed and external libraries Managed items are stored by Frameleaf. External library items point at files you manage yourself. Recovery for external libraries is off by default. When you allow it, a verified matching copy is stored under Frameleaf's management and the item keeps its identity; the original external p

A separate downloader fetches and verifies the models into a cache, without ever seeing your library. articles.text: Model staging lets your machine-learning worker run with no internet access at all. A separate downloader fetches and verifies the models into a cache, without ever seeing your library. The inference worker then reads those verified models from the cache and never downloads anything itself. It's an advanced option for locked-down installations; ordinary online and trusted remote workers work as before. Use your release's docker-compose.ml-isolated.yml and its matching staging command. Your host needs to support the Compose overrides and network isolation that file uses; on a NAS, use an equivalent host firewall instead. Keep the isolation settings in place and check that your host enforces them, because that isolation is the point of this mode. Prepare the worker Keep your existing Compose project, model cache and hardware settings. Use the same release and hardware variant for the downloader and inference worker. Put machine-learning runtime settings in .env.ml and model-source settings in model-staging.env. Neither file needs database, backup or Cloud provisioning credentials, or media folders. Validate the complete Compose configuration on the target host before changing the running worker. Stop inference before acquiring, refreshing or rolling back its models. Your other server services can keep running. See Hardware acceleration and Workers and where jobs run for choosing the worker and its device. Download and verify a model From the installation directory, using the release's regular Compose file: The example stages a model for a CUDA description worker. Use the task, model and acceleration configured for your own installation. Rootless installations use their matching Compose file and cache-owner settings. Stage each configured model, including fallback models. Smart search needs both visual and textual models; faces and text recognition each need detection and recognition. Semantic masks and restoration have their own provisioning steps in the matching release. Staging verifies model files without processing photos or loading custom model code. Each model gets a verification receipt that catches any later change to its files, on top of the release's trusted origin and pinned model information. Offline jobs and errors Once staged, the verified cache serves local inference with no internet connection. Run your configured jobs once to confirm each one has its model. The worker stays strict about what it loads: A missing or changed file produces a clear error instead of an automatic download. A mirror that lacks the pinned files is refused rather than swapped for another source. Custom models need an explicit trust decision on the worker itself; choosing one in the web interface isn't enough. Existing unverified caches need restaging. The old directory is kept, but isn't used as a fallback. If a job can't load its model, check the recorded error, cache permissions, selected model and worker version. Keep your working cache while you troubleshoot. Refresh and recovery To update a model, stop inference and rerun the same acquisition command with --refresh. It downloads and verifies the update; if the download fails, your active cache stays as it was. A successful refresh keeps one previous staged copy, so you can go back with --rollback and the same task, model and options. A new pinned revision can use a different cache directory, so keep the previous matching release and cache until you've checked the new one. Rolling back a model only affects that model, not your library database, application release or edits.

articles.text: Moving to new hardware is safe and resumable, and you finish with a checksum-verified report before you retire anything. There are two ways to do it: Move the whole server. Copy your files and restore a database backup on the new machine. See Backup and restore. If the media folder ends up at a different path inside the container, see Change the media location below. Move one person's library to a different, already running server. That's what this page covers. If you use Cloud Backup, you can also move the whole server from a complete independent export, then recover it on the new server without Cloud access. Keep its recovery file, media, configuration and keys private. See Export and recover without Cloud access. The database dump in the export is restored as a separate step. A library move uses the migrate command of the Frameleaf command-line tool. It runs on a computer you control, copies everything over the API, and ends with an audit you review before you retire the old server. Your old server stays exactly as it is: the move never deletes anything there, and you decide when to retire it. The web app doesn't run migrations or ask for API keys. How it works Preflight checks both connections, the API key permissions and the owner on each side. It changes nothing. Dry run lists what would move and what the new server already has. It writes nothing. Run copies originals, then albums (with their collections), tags, stacks and people. Every finished item is saved to a local ledger file, so an interrupted run resumes where it stopped. Retry tries failed originals again, adds them to their albums and tags, and reattaches names to faces. Verify checks every original on the new server by checksum, without contacting the old one, and writes an audit report. Before you start Move one person at a time. You need an API key for that person on both servers. A key can only read and write its own account's library, so an administrator's key would copy the photos into the administrator's account. Sign in as the person on each server, open Settings, then Access & security, then API keys, and create a key with these permissions (or all): Without the optional permissions, stacks and people are skipped and everything else still moves. If the account doesn't exist on the new server yet, create it first. Enter the addresses and keys Type each key when the terminal waits for it. Nothing is shown as you type, and the key stays out of your shell history. The variable names are the tool's own and can't be changed, and no command takes a key as an argument. Preflight and dry run Preflight stops on any missing required permission and warns if the two accounts have different email addresses (everything ends up owned by the new server's account). It doesn't create a ledger. If an existing ledger was made for a different pair of servers, use a different --ledger path. The dry run fills the ledger with what's on the old server and asks the new one which originals it already has. Its report is marked as a dry run and never shows a pass. Run the move --serve adds a progress page at http://127.0.0.1:2285 where you can pause, resume or stop. Closing the page doesn't stop the move. If the run stops for any reason (Ctrl+C, a reboot, a dropped connection), just run the same command again. The ledger skips everything already done. Keep the ledger file until you've retired the old server. Albums, tags and stacks are only marked complete once every one of their photos is on the new server. If an original failed, its albums stay pending until it arrives. articles.title: Physical deduplication
articles.description: Store one copy of a file that several people on your server uploaded, while each keeps their own photo, albums and permissions.
articles.intro: In a family, the same photo often ends up in several people's libraries: shared holiday pictures, copied phone backups, the same Google Photos export imported twice. Frameleaf keeps one stored copy of an identical file, while every account keeps its own photo in its own library. You win back disk space and nobody notices a thing.

headings.title: How it works
headings.text: It's always on, and there's nothing to switch on or choose. Settings, then Storage & originals, then Originals & folder structure says so under One file per photo.

headings.title: Convert an existing library
headings.text: Open Settings, then Library care, then Identical files (save space). You can also select Library Care at the bottom of the sidebar.

headings.title: While a plan is applied
headings.text: Applying is a background job. It's listed in Activity and the notifications panel of the administrator who applied it, and on the Identical files (save space) page for every administrator. The administrator who applied it can pause, resume or stop it. It survives closing the browser and restarting the server, and carries on from the last copy it finished.

headings.title: Workers
headings.text: Physical deduplication only runs on your server's own workers. A render worker can only take Studio exports and previews, restorations and quick edits, never this job. See Workers and where jobs run.

articles.text: In a family, the same photo often ends up in several people's libraries: shared holiday pictures, copied phone backups, the same Google Photos export imported twice. Frameleaf keeps one stored copy of an identical file, while every account keeps its own photo in its own library. You win back disk space and nobody notices a thing. Ownership stays exactly as it was. Each photo keeps its owner, albums, favourites, descriptions, faces, stacks, shared links, Locked state and permissions; only the file on disk it points at changes. Libraries stay separate, so this is different from partner sharing. Every library is still charged the full size of its photos. For reviewing duplicates within one library, see Duplicates. Applying a plan moves redundant files out of your library after checking them, so make an independent, verified backup first. Once files are shared, that one original is worth backing up even more carefully. How it works It's always on, and there's nothing to switch on or choose. Settings, then Storage & originals, then Originals & folder structure says so under One file per photo. New uploads are handled automatically. After the server has worked out an upload's checksum, it reuses the file the server already keeps if any library already holds an exact copy with the same checksum and size. Otherwise the upload is stored as normal. Files already on the server are converted with a reviewed plan, described below. Uploads are still checked for duplicates inside the uploader's own library, as before. Copies across accounts aren't refused at upload. External library files are never moved, linked or deleted. A stored file that no library uses any more isn't deleted. It waits in File trash in Library Care, where an administrator can restore it or delete it permanently. Convert an existing library Open Settings, then Library care, then Identical files (save space). You can also select Library Care at the bottom of the sidebar. Prepare a preview Choose: Scan scope: All accounts, or one account's copies. Retain originals in: the account whose originals are kept. Usually this is the household account whose folder layout you want shared files to follow. It can't also be the scan scope. Then select Prepare preview plan. The preview runs in the background and changes no files. It lists every exact copy next to the retained original it matches, grouped by original, with: the checksum (SHA-1 for older uploads, SHA-256 for newer ones) and size of the copy and the original how many photos point at the original now, and after the plan the decision for each copy: share the retained original, or skip it with a reason, such as external library, no exact copy in the retained account, already shared, or size unavailable Each plan is named after a fingerprint of its evidence, for example PD-1A2B3C4D. Preparing a new preview replaces the plan, with a new name. The list holds the first 500 copies. The totals cover everything, but only the listed copies are applied. Afterwards, prepare another plan for the rest; copies already shared are skipped. Another account's Locked media is never listed. Its copies are counted (for example "2 copies are another account's Locked media"), included in the plan and checked like any other, but their names, paths and thumbnails are only shown to their owner in an unlocked session. Decide per group Each group has Share this original in the plan. Clear it to leave that group alone: its copies keep their own files. Mark the plan reviewed Select Mark plan reviewed. The server checks the plan against the library again, and refuses (changing nothing) when: a newer preview replaced the plan, or the plan was already applied, fully or partly any copy or original in the plan was removed, trashed, moved to another account, or changed path, checksum or size a copy already points at its original the original gained or lost references since the preview If anything changed, the page shows the current state and you simply prepare

articles.title: Remote access on your own
articles.description: Reach your self-hosted server away from home with a VPN, Tailscale or your own reverse proxy, without Frameleaf Cloud.
articles.intro: Your photos are just as easy to reach on holiday as on your sofa. There are two ways to connect to your Frameleaf server away from home:

headings.title: Option 1: a VPN to your home network
headings.text: A VPN such as WireGuard or OpenVPN opens an encrypted connection from your phone or laptop to your home network. You then reach Frameleaf by its home address, exactly as you do at home.

headings.title: Option 2: Tailscale
headings.text: If you can't open a port on your router, Tailscale connects your devices with WireGuard tunnels, even when both ends are behind a home router.

headings.title: Option 3: your own reverse proxy
headings.text: A reverse proxy serves Frameleaf over HTTPS at your own address, such as https://photos.example.com, just like any other website. This makes most sense if you have your own domain; a dynamic DNS name works too. The Frameleaf apps can then connect from anywhere with no VPN app.

headings.title: After you set it up
headings.text: Set Public server URL in Settings, then Frameleaf Cloud, then Remote access to the address people use from outside. Shared links, emails and sign-in callbacks use it. It works without a Frameleaf Cloud link. Leave off the trailing slash. If you use your own sign-in provider, add the new address to its redirect URIs. In the Frameleaf apps, add the outside address so they can connect away from home.

articles.text: Your photos are just as easy to reach on holiday as on your sofa. There are two ways to connect to your Frameleaf server away from home: Frameleaf Cloud remote access: a direct connection with HTTPS and a stable address, which a Server licence sets up for you, plus the relay with a Cloud plan for no router changes. See Remote access with Frameleaf Cloud. Set it up yourself, with one of the options on this page. Nothing here needs Frameleaf Cloud. Never forward port 2283 straight to the internet. That exposes the web app over plain HTTP, so anyone between you and your server could read or change your traffic, including your password. Option 1: a VPN to your home network A VPN such as WireGuard or OpenVPN opens an encrypted connection from your phone or laptop to your home network. You then reach Frameleaf by its home address, exactly as you do at home. Good: Only devices you allow onto your VPN can reach Frameleaf. Keep the VPN and Frameleaf updated. Not so good: Without a fixed IP address at home, you need a dynamic DNS service. The VPN app has to be installed and on, on every device. You need to open a port on your router for the VPN. Option 2: Tailscale If you can't open a port on your router, Tailscale connects your devices with WireGuard tunnels, even when both ends are behind a home router. Good: Very little setup on the server and on your devices. Frameleaf isn't exposed to the internet. Not so good: The Tailscale app usually runs with full system rights on your devices, which adds a little risk compared with a plain WireGuard server. It's a paid service, with a free tier for personal use. It has to be installed and running on the server and every device. Option 3: your own reverse proxy A reverse proxy serves Frameleaf over HTTPS at your own address, such as https://photos.example.com, just like any other website. This makes most sense if you have your own domain; a dynamic DNS name works too. The Frameleaf apps can then connect from anywhere with no VPN app. You'll need a certificate. Let's Encrypt gives free certificates and is what we recommend for anything reachable from the internet. A self-signed certificate also encrypts traffic, but browsers show a warning. If you use a hosted proxy, check its upload limits, privacy terms and media-service restrictions. See Reverse proxy for the headers, upload limits and example configurations. Good: Nothing extra to install on your devices. If you only need the web app remotely, you can put an access control service in front of it to shield Frameleaf from the internet. Not so good: More involved to set up. Depending on your setup, the web app and API are exposed to the internet, so keep Frameleaf up to date. After you set it up Set Public server URL in Settings, then Frameleaf Cloud, then Remote access to the address people use from outside. Shared links, emails and sign-in callbacks use it. It works without a Frameleaf Cloud link. Leave off the trailing slash. If you use your own sign-in provider, add the new address to its redirect URIs. In the Frameleaf apps, add the outside address so they can connect away from home. A new server can only be set up from your home network. If the server isn't at home, such as a rented server, connect through an SSH tunnel to set it up, or add your network to FRAMELEAF_TRUSTED_LAN_CIDRS. See Setting up a new server.

articles.title: Remote machine learning
articles.description: Run Frameleaf's machine learning on a more powerful computer on your network.
articles.intro: Got a small server, such as a Raspberry Pi, and a more powerful desktop or laptop nearby? Run Frameleaf's machine learning container on the bigger computer and get faster smart search and face detection without upgrading your server. The server sends image previews to that computer for processing, and the machine learning container doesn't keep them or link them to a user.

headings.title: Set it up
headings.text: Install Docker on the remote computer. Save this as docker-compose.yml on the remote computer:

headings.title: Route work to the remote computer
headings.text: Each address in the list becomes a destination. Library work that has no route yet goes to the first address in the list; the order sets nothing else. articles.text: Got a small server, such as a Raspberry Pi, and a more powerful desktop or laptop nearby? Run Frameleaf's machine learning container on the bigger computer and get faster smart search and face detection without upgrading your server. The server sends image previews to that computer for processing, and the machine learning container doesn't keep them or link them to a user. Smart search and face detection use the remote container. Grouping faces into people doesn't, because it works from results already saved in the database. Image previews are sent to the remote computer, so use a computer you trust rather than a shared machine or a paid cloud service. Keep the worker on a trusted network and restrict which hosts can reach it. To require authentication, set FRAMELEAF_ML_AUTH_TOKEN on the worker and the matching credential on its processing destination. Use HTTPS across untrusted networks. Set it up Install Docker on the remote computer. Save this as docker-compose.yml on the remote computer: Start it with docker compose up -d. On your Frameleaf server, go to Settings, then Search & intelligence, and open Advanced: the helper program’s address. Click Add address, enter the remote container's address, for example http://192.168.1.50:3003, and select Save changes. You can also add it in Settings, then Computers & background work, then Computers: choose Add a computer, then Connect by address. Each address becomes a destination you can route work to and check. See Workers and where jobs run. To use a GPU on the remote computer, also add hwaccel.ml.yml and follow Hardware acceleration. Keep both computers on the same Frameleaf version. Update the remote container whenever you upgrade the server. Route work to the remote computer Each address in the list becomes a destination. To send work to the remote computer, choose it for each kind of work (faces, visual search, text, descriptions) in Settings, then Computers & background work, then Where work runs. See Workers and where jobs run. Work goes exactly where you route it. If the remote computer is off, jobs routed to it are refused and say why, rather than being sent to the local container. Smart search and face detection then don't run for new photos, and neither do duplicate detection and face grouping, which depend on them. When the remote computer is back, open Settings, then Computers & background work, then Background work, and choose Catch up for Preparing photos for search and Finding faces. If everything runs on the remote computer, you can remove the local address and the immich-machine-learning service from your server's Compose file to save resources. At least one address must stay in the list. Several machine learning computers Each kind of work goes to one destination. To share one kind of work across several computers, put a load balancer in front of them and use its address for that work. That also lets you mix configurations on one computer, for example an OpenVINO container next to a CUDA one, or a CPU container alongside a GPU one to use both. One machine learning container can serve several Frameleaf servers, even if they use different models, though that raises peak memory use.

articles.title: Reverse proxy
articles.description: Put Frameleaf behind nginx, Caddy, Apache or Traefik for HTTPS on your own domain, with the headers, upload sizes and timeouts it needs.
articles.intro: A reverse proxy sits in front of Frameleaf and passes requests on to it. It's the usual way to serve Frameleaf over HTTPS on your own domain, such as https://photos.example.com, and it can handle certificates, load balancing and access control for you.

headings.title: What every proxy needs
headings.text: Forward all headers, and set Host, X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-For to the right values. Allow large uploads. Videos can be many gigabytes. Long timeouts. Large uploads fail if the proxy gives up after a minute. WebSockets. The web app uses them for live updates. Serve Frameleaf at the root of a domain or subdomain. Frameleaf can't be served on a sub-path such as https://example.com/photos.

The apps can't make these credentials, so you create them and give one to each person, who adds it in the app's connection options: see iPhone and iPad and Android.

articles.title: Scaling
articles.description: Run Frameleaf across several containers or machines, and scale back down when you need the hardware for something else.
articles.intro: The Frameleaf server is built so that several copies can run side by side. Put a gaming PC to work on transcoding and thumbnails, or spread the load across a small cluster, then hand the hardware back whenever you need it.

headings.title: Background workers only
headings.text: Each server container runs an API worker, a job worker and an edge worker for remote access. If you're adding machines only to get through background work faster, turn off the API on them with FRAMELEAF_WORKERS_EXCLUDE: 'api'. See Split the server into containers.

headings.title: Scaling down
headings.text: You can scale down just as easily. All state lives in PostgreSQL and the file system, so it's safe to stop a server container, for example to free your GPU for a game. As long as one container runs the API worker, you can still browse Frameleaf, and jobs wait until a worker is available to process them.

articles.text: The Frameleaf server is built so that several copies can run side by side. Put a gaming PC to work on transcoding and thumbnails, or spread the load across a small cluster, then hand the hardware back whenever you need it. The one requirement is that every copy uses the same shared infrastructure: the same PostgreSQL database the same files, mounted at the same path in every container On a single machine, one container already runs several background jobs at once. To get more done, raise Concurrency rather than adding containers. Each machine needs secure access to the shared database and media mounts. Keep the PostgreSQL data directory on local disk, even when your media is on a network share. The exact steps depend on your own infrastructure, so this works best if you're comfortable managing it. Background workers only Each server container runs an API worker, a job worker and an edge worker for remote access. If you're adding machines only to get through background work faster, turn off the API on them with FRAMELEAF_WORKERS_EXCLUDE: 'api'. See Split the server into containers. Machine learning scales separately: run more machine learning containers and put a load balancer in front of them. See Remote machine learning and Workers and where jobs run. Scaling down You can scale down just as easily. All state lives in PostgreSQL and the file system, so it's safe to stop a server container, for example to free your GPU for a game. As long as one container runs the API worker, you can still browse Frameleaf, and jobs wait until a worker is available to process them. When a container stops, running jobs get a short grace period and then go back to waiting. See Stopping the server.

Keep the complete recovery key file on another device. For client-encrypted backups it contains every root-key version used by retained backups and trusted snapshot history. It's complete once its checks for missing or corrupt references pass. For client-encrypted recovery, the trusted history in the complete key file picks the right snapshot for you. articles.title: System integrity
articles.description: How Frameleaf checks that your library files are intact, what the integrity reports mean, and the start-up checks on your storage folders.
articles.intro: Frameleaf keeps an eye on your library for you, so you hear about a missing or damaged file long before you need it. It checks your storage in two ways: integrity checks run on a schedule and look for missing, unknown and changed files, and folder checks run every time the server starts to make sure it can read and write its storage.

headings.text: There are three checks. They only read your library and never change a file.

headings.title: Folder checks at start-up

articles.text: Frameleaf keeps an eye on your library for you, so you hear about a missing or damaged file long before you need it. It checks your storage in two ways: integrity checks run on a schedule and look for missing, unknown and changed files, and folder checks run every time the server starts to make sure it can read and write its storage. Integrity checks There are three checks. They only read your library and never change a file. Schedule All three run every night at 3:00 AM by default. Change the schedule, or turn a check off, in Settings, then Library care, then File checks. The checksum check reads every byte of every file, so it's the heaviest. It has two extra limits, so it can work through a large library over a few nights instead of all at once: The checks run in the Integrity checks queue, one at a time. Review the reports See the results in Settings, then Library care, then File checks. Each check shows when it last ran and how many findings it has. Run check runs one check in full now. Run all checks runs all three. View report lists the findings. Filter them by path, or download the report file. Recheck findings looks only at the items already reported and clears those that are fixed. It's much quicker than a full check. You can delete a single finding or a whole report. For untracked files, this deletes the file from disk and can't be undone. For missing files and checksum mismatches, the item is moved to the trash, or its generated file is removed. The same checks are available as maintenance jobs in Settings, then Computers & background work, then Background work, then More tasks: Find missing files, Find untracked files and Verify checksums, each with a recheck. Each also has a job that acts on every finding at once, and these change your files: Move photos with missing files to Trash, Move photos with checksum mismatches to Trash, and Delete untracked files from disk, which can't be undone. Check files for damage under Run a task now starts the checksum check. What usually causes each finding Untracked files are the most common. Usually they're thumbnails or encoded videos that were only partly created and never cleaned up. You can delete those, because Frameleaf can make them again. For anything else, check whether the photo is already in Frameleaf and how the file got there. In Background work, choose Catch up for Making thumbnails and Converting videos so every item has its thumbnails and encoded videos. The server logs show any items that have problems while they run. Missing files are files the database expects but can't find. Usually a file was deleted from the library folder on disk (Frameleaf doesn't support that), or a drive isn't mounted. Find the cause before you act on them. To track down a file that has moved, see Recover missing or damaged media. Checksum mismatches often point to file system corruption. They also appear when a file in the library folder was edited directly, which Frameleaf doesn't support. Look at each item to see whether it or its metadata changed. If a file was edited on purpose, delete it from Frameleaf and upload it again as a new item. Deleting an untracked file removes it from disk for good. Check each file before you delete it. Folder checks at start-up Every time the server starts, it checks that it can read and write each of its storage folders: upload/, library/, thumbs/, encoded-video/, profile/ and backups/. For each folder it: creates a hidden marker file named .immich, the first time reads the marker file overwrites the marker file If any step fails, the server doesn't start. This catches two common problems: Wrong permissions: the server can't read or write the folder. A missing mount: the marker file should be there but isn't, which usually means a volume isn't mounted where it was before. The .immich files help Frameleaf recognise its folders. Leave them in place, apart from the cases below. Missing marker files An error like this means the server wrote marker files
