headings.title: Setting up a new server
headings.text: A new server has no administrator. Until it has one, anyone on its home network can claim it; there is no setup code. Set it up soon after installing, before anyone else on your network reaches it.

articles.text: Every server-wide setting lives in one place, the Command Center, and you can review all your changes before you save them. Select Settings in the sidebar, then open the area you need. Only administrators see these sections; everyone else sees their own preferences. This page walks through the server settings area by area. Each setting also has a key in the config file, shown in brackets where it helps. Saving changes Every settings page edits one shared draft. You can change things on several pages and save them together. Review changes lists every change with its page, the saved value and the new value. Save changes saves them all at once. Discard returns every page to the saved settings. Reset this page puts that page's defaults into the draft; they're applied when you save. Pages with unsaved changes are marked in the settings list. Leaving with unsaved changes asks whether to keep editing or discard them. Reloading the tab brings the draft back, except passwords, keys and addresses that contain credentials. Those are never stored in the browser. If another administrator saves while you're editing, your draft is kept. Changes to different settings are carried onto theirs and you save again. If you both changed the same setting, the page shows the saved value and yours side by side: keep your changes on top of the latest settings, or discard your draft and load the latest. Actions that do something straight away, such as sending a test email or unlinking all OAuth accounts, run on their own. Sending a test email also saves the email settings, and nothing else. Configuration transfer Server & updates, then Configuration transfer lets you review, copy, import or export the saved settings: Export as JSON and Copy to clipboard leave out passwords, secrets and keys. Import from JSON puts the file's settings into your draft so you can review them before saving. Settings this server doesn't have are listed and ignored, and credentials in the file are never applied. If you'd rather manage settings from a file on disk, see Config file. Change history Change history lists every change saved from the settings pages, including credential changes, newest first. Each entry shows the administrator who saved it, the time, and each setting before and after. It's kept on the server, so every administrator sees the same list of the latest 50 saves. Credentials only ever appear as replaced or cleared. Server credentials The OAuth client secret and the SMTP password are write-only. Their rows show Stored or Not set, never the value itself. Replace credential opens a dialog with a single field. The value is sent once, checked like any other change (a new SMTP password is tested against the mail server, for example), and cleared from the dialog when it closes. Clear removes the stored value after you confirm. Saving any other setting, copying, exporting or importing never carries a credential. A stored secret never follows a change of server. Saving a different mail server host or username clears the SMTP password, and saving a different OAuth issuer URL clears the client secret. Replace the credential for the new server afterwards. Send test email uses the stored SMTP password as long as the server, port, username and security settings on the page match the saved ones. Every replacement or removal is written to the server log by credential name and administrator, never by value. If email is turned on and the new mail server needs a password: turn email off, save the new server, replace the password, then turn email on again. Scripts can use GET /api/admin/config/credentials to see which credentials are stored, and PUT or DELETE /api/admin/config/credentials/{name} to replace or clear one. While a config file manages the settings, credentials come from that file and can't be changed in the Command Center. Storage & originals Trash We recommend keeping the trash on. With it off, everything you delete is removed permanently, straight away. Delete d

articles.title: Upgrading
articles.description: Update the Synology package in Package Center and your library with Manager, or move a manual installation to a new Compose release.
articles.intro: Each Frameleaf release brings new features and fixes, and upgrading takes a few minutes. Manager and the Synology app check the release, take a database checkpoint and walk you through each step.

headings.title: With the Synology app
headings.text: The Synology package and your photo library update separately:

headings.title: With Frameleaf Manager
headings.text: Open Manager and choose Updates. Select an Eligible release. Updates lists only releases newer than the one running; when there are none, it shows Up to date. Select Verify and review update and read the recovery information. Select Update Frameleaf, then select Update Frameleaf again in the confirmation dialog. When it finishes, open Frameleaf and check sign-in, albums, several originals and background processing.

headings.title: With Docker Compose
headings.text: Keep the same project folder, .env, storage paths, external-library mounts and volume names. Download the matching release files and look over their changes before you replace your Compose file. Use the database image that the matching Compose file specifies.

headings.title: First start after an update
headings.text: On a large library, database migrations and indexes can take a while. Leave the server running while it makes progress without errors. Machine learning downloads any new models the first time they're used.

headings.title: Version tags
headings.text: Hardware-specific machine learning tags add a suffix such as -cuda or -openvino. Keep the suffix when you change the release version.

headings.title: Recover after a failed update
headings.text: Keep the failed installation as it is and read the release's recovery instructions. An older server can't always read a database that a newer release has changed.

articles.text: Each Frameleaf release brings new features and fixes, and upgrading takes a few minutes. Manager and the Synology app check the release, take a database checkpoint and walk you through each step. Before you start, read the release notes and back up both your database and your media. A database backup on its own can't undo changes to your media, so you need both. With the Synology app The Synology package and your photo library update separately: Get the newer Frameleaf Manager SPK from Frameleaf, with its checksum. Verify the file, then upload it with Package Center → Manual Install. The upgrade keeps your storage folders, HTTPS hostname and ports, so leave those folders in place. Open the app from the DSM main menu. In Updates, choose Review update beside an eligible photo-library release. Review the release, database checkpoint, storage and service changes, then confirm the update. Check Activity for the result. Then open your library and check that sign-in, a few originals, videos and background processing all work. If an operation is interrupted, use the recovery action recorded in Activity. Keep everything in the Synology app: don't create a separate Container Manager project or switch database images on upgraded files. See Synology for removing the package and what data it keeps. With Frameleaf Manager Open Manager and choose Updates. Select an Eligible release. Updates lists only releases newer than the one running; when there are none, it shows Up to date. Select Verify and review update and read the recovery information. Select Update Frameleaf, then select Update Frameleaf again in the confirmation dialog. When it finishes, open Frameleaf and check sign-in, albums, several originals and background processing. Manager downloads compatible images and creates a database checkpoint before it applies the release. If an operation fails, its error tells you why; fix the cause and select Resume safely. Cancel update and restart is offered while it's still safe to go back to the previous release. Once the new release may have changed the database or media, recovery continues forward, because switching back to an older image isn't a safe rollback. To return to an earlier state, restore a database recovery point from Backups; Manager restores it with its matching release. See Restore a Manager backup. With Docker Compose Keep the same project folder, .env, storage paths, external-library mounts and volume names. Download the matching release files and look over their changes before you replace your Compose file. Use the database image that the matching Compose file specifies. Make sure your database and media backups are usable. Use FRAMELEAF_VERSION=latest for the current release, or an exact release tag when you want a fixed version. If the new bundle renames the application service to frameleaf-server, run docker compose down with your current Compose file, before you replace it. Leave off --volumes and -v so your database, media and named volumes stay. Keep the project name, and update custom overrides, proxy targets and scripts to use frameleaf-server. Replace the Compose files with the matching release files, then run these from the existing Compose folder: Update any separate machine learning container to the matching release too. The app download page and release notes list which app versions work with the new server. Run only one stack against a PostgreSQL directory, and never use docker compose down --volumes during an upgrade. First start after an update On a large library, database migrations and indexes can take a while. Leave the server running while it makes progress without errors. Machine learning downloads any new models the first time they're used. Then open a few photos, videos and albums, and check the jobs page for failures. That tells you your library has finished processing, which a healthy container alone doesn't. Version tags Hardware-specific machine learning tags add a suffix such as -cuda or -openvi

You can search by name or email, filter to Active, Administrators or Deleted accounts, and sort by name, newest first or storage used. Select an account to open its details. Leave it blank for no limit. set a Storage label, used as their folder name on disk (see below). choose the Role: User or Administrator. turn on Require a password change at the next sign-in. set an Initial six-digit PIN for Locked content, if they need one before their first sign-in. Its owner can change it later. turn on Send a welcome email. This only appears once email is set up. Select Create account. Invite people with their Frameleaf account When your server is linked to Frameleaf Cloud, you can invite people from your Frameleaf account instead of creating a password for them. An invited person gets their own account and library the first time they use Sign in with Frameleaf, on the web or in the Frameleaf app. Being invited doesn't show them your library; share items, albums or Spaces with them for that. New invited accounts start with the Storage quota for invited accounts, set in Settings, then Access & security, then Sign in with Frameleaf. It's unlimited by default, so their phone can back up straight away. The setting only applies to accounts created after you change it, and the server's owner is never given it. When you or Frameleaf Cloud remove someone's access, their Frameleaf sign-ins on your server end. Their account and library stay until you delete the account. See Share a server with people. Edit an account Open an account and select Edit account to change its name, email, avatar colour, role, quota or storage label, then Save account. If someone else changed the account since you opened it, you're asked to reopen it to see the latest details. To keep you from locking yourself out, you can't delete your own administrator account or remove your own administrator role while you're signed in with it. Storage quotas A quota limits how much a person can upload. Once they reach it, new uploads stop; their existing photos stay. Leave the quota blank for no limit. A quota of 0 blocks new uploads while keeping existing photos. A quota doesn't reserve disk space, so you can set quotas that add up to more than your disk holds. Files in external libraries don't count towards a quota. Storage labels By default each person's files are stored in a folder named after their account ID. A storage label replaces that with a name you choose, using letters, numbers, hyphens or underscores. It's used by the storage template. Changing the label doesn't move files that are already stored. Run the Storage organization job when you're ready. Turn off casting Allow casting controls whether the account can use Google Cast. When it's off, the person can't turn casting back on themselves. Sign-in and security Reset a password Open the account and select Reset password. Select Generate temporary password. Copy the temporary password and give it to them. It's shown only once. Their old password stops working, and they must choose a new one when they next sign in. Reset or set a Locked PIN Under Locked folder PIN: Reset PIN clears the person's PIN so they can set a new one after signing in. Set PIN sets a new six-digit PIN for them. Either way, every device signed in to the account is signed out of Locked con

articles.title: Video transcoding
articles.description: How Frameleaf makes playback copies of your videos, what each transcoding setting does, and how to use a GPU for it.
articles.intro: Your videos play smoothly on every device, and your originals stay exactly as you shot them. Frameleaf makes a playback copy when the original won't play well everywhere, for example because of its codec, container or resolution. Playback copies are stored in UPLOAD_LOCATION/encoded-video and can always be made again. They're created by the Playback videos job queue.

headings.title: Settings
headings.text: Find these in Settings, then Editing & playback, then Video playback copies.

headings.title: Hardware transcoding
headings.text: A GPU takes most of the transcoding work off the processor, so videos are ready sooner and the server stays free for everything else.

articles.text: Your videos play smoothly on every device, and your originals stay exactly as you shot them. Frameleaf makes a playback copy when the original won't play well everywhere, for example because of its codec, container or resolution. Playback copies are stored in UPLOAD_LOCATION/encoded-video and can always be made again. They're created by the Playback videos job queue. Edits you render in the editor and Studio exports use the same transcoding settings, including hardware acceleration. When an edit needs filters that only run on the processor, rendering switches to software by itself. Settings Find these in Settings, then Editing & playback, then Video playback copies. Transcode policy The policy decides which videos get a playback copy. HDR videos and videos with a pixel format other than YUV 4:2:0 are always transcoded, unless transcoding is turned off. Encoding options The advanced options (maximum B-frames, reference frames, maximum keyframe interval, temporal AQ, constant quality mode, preferred hardware device) have sensible defaults, so you rarely need to change them. Temporal AQ applies only to NVENC; the preferred hardware device applies only to VAAPI and Quick Sync and picks the /dev/dri node to use. Real-time transcoding Real-time Transcoding is experimental. It transcodes while a video streams, so the player can switch quality. On a server that can't keep up, it can add latency and stuttering. It's off by default. When on, it offers H.264 and HEVC at 480p, 720p and 1080p; choose only codecs your accelerator can encode if you use one. Hardware transcoding A GPU takes most of the transcoding work off the processor, so videos are ready sooner and the server stays free for everything else. Supported hardware Not supported: Raspberry Pi, and Quick Sync under WSL2. VAAPI works on NVIDIA and Intel too, but the specific options are better optimised for their own hardware. Codec support depends on the hardware. H.264 and HEVC usually work; NVIDIA and AMD GPUs can't encode VP9. Newer devices tend to give better quality. Hardware transcoding makes noticeably larger files than software transcoding at similar settings, usually at lower quality. Slower presets and more efficient codecs narrow the gap. If hardware transcoding fails for a video, Frameleaf transcodes it in software instead. Before you start NVENC The official NVIDIA driver. On Linux (not WSL2), the NVIDIA Container Toolkit. Quick Sync VP9 needs a 9th generation Intel CPU or newer. 11th generation and older CPUs may need low-power encoding turned on in the host's graphics driver for VP9. An 11th generation CPU on kernel 5.15 (as shipped with Ubuntu 22.04 LTS) needs a newer kernel. RKMPP A supported Rockchip SoC. Only RK3588 does tone-mapping in hardware; others tone-map in software but still encode in hardware. Hardware tone-mapping needs /usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libmali.so.1 on the host. Install the libmali release for your Mali GPU (libmali-valhall-g610-g13p0-gbm on RK3588), then in hwaccel.transcoding.yml, under rkmpp, uncomment these three lines: Set it up These steps are for manual Docker Compose installations. hwaccel.transcoding.yml is Frameleaf's hardware-acceleration helper: it supplies the GPU device mappings and runtime options for the supported backends. It comes with the release assets; use the one from the same release as your Compose file. If you prefer a single Compose file, use the inline configuration below instead of downloading the helper. If the helper isn't already in your release bundle, download hwaccel.transcoding.yml into the same folder as docker-compose.yml. The link follows the latest published release; for an older installation, use its matching release asset. In docker-compose.yml, under services → frameleaf-server, uncomment the extends section and change cpu to nvenc, quicksync, rkmpp, vaapi or vaapi-wsl. Keep the service's existing image, volumes, environment and ports. Run docker compose up -d frameleaf-server to recreate the server

articles.title: Workers and where jobs run
articles.description: Add GPU computers on your network, see every computer's state, choose where each kind of work runs and how heavy a model it uses, and decide what may run in the cloud.
articles.intro: Put the graphics card in your desktop to work for your photo library. Frameleaf can hand heavy work such as faces, search and descriptions to other computers on your network, so it finishes faster and your server stays responsive. You decide, for each kind of work, where it runs and how heavy a model it uses, and work only ever runs where you've sent it.

headings.title: Check your hardware first
headings.text: Settings, then Computers & background work, then Graphics card check tells you whether a graphics card is speeding up video and AI features, and how to fix it if not. Measure this server's speed runs a two-minute test that times search, a transcode, descriptions and restoration. See Hardware acceleration.

headings.title: Two kinds of worker
headings.text: Library analysis and restoration never share a worker.

Each row says whether it works on this server, and you pick where it runs:

headings.text: Start a long job and walk away. Studio renders, edits, restorations, bulk changes, description runs, Library Care scans, imports and physical deduplication keep running when you close the browser, and carry on after a server restart.

headings.title: For scripts
headings.text: GET /api/admin/workers returns the inventory to administrators. It reads stored state only: loads are counts, runners are process names, and no owner, item or credential is returned. Destinations, routes and checks use the /api/ml-destinations endpoints.

articles.text: Put the graphics card in your desktop to work for your photo library. Frameleaf can hand heavy work such as faces, search and descriptions to other computers on your network, so it finishes faster and your server stays responsive. You decide, for each kind of work, where it runs and how heavy a model it uses, and work only ever runs where you've sent it. Machine learning work goes to destinations: the machine learning container that ships with the server, and other machines on your network. Open Settings, then Computers & background work: Computers lists this server and every computer that helps it, with its state, and is where you add a computer Where work runs chooses which computer does each kind of heavy work For the jobs that run inside the server itself, see Jobs and queues. Check your hardware first Settings, then Computers & background work, then Graphics card check tells you whether a graphics card is speeding up video and AI features, and how to fix it if not. Measure this server's speed runs a two-minute test that times search, a transcode, descriptions and restoration. See Hardware acceleration. Two kinds of worker Library analysis and restoration never share a worker. Studio helpers, computers running Frameleaf's Studio helper, handle Studio exports and previews. The server enforces these rules: A destination on this server or your network may do library analysis or restoration, not both. Ticking one kind in the form closes the other. A restoration is refused, never moved, if its destination is still allowed both kinds of work from before this rule, or points at an address that library analysis is routed to. Destinations saved before the rule that allow both kinds keep running library analysis, and are listed under Workers allowed both kinds of work until you limit them to one. If a job's destination is missing, turned off or unreachable, the job is refused and says why. It isn't quietly sent somewhere else. Computers Computers starts with a sentence that says whether every computer is answering. Below it, the list shows This server, which is built in and can't be removed, and each computer that helps it. A computer is listed once, with one state: Each row also says what the computer helps with (AI features, Studio and restoration) and how many kinds of work are set to run there. Manage opens its details. Add a computer Add a computer offers two ways to connect one: For AI features: connect by address. For a computer already running Frameleaf's AI service, including Linux. Choose Connect by address, type its address, for example http://192.168.1.40:3003, and an access key if it has one, then tick what it may do. For Studio exports and AI restoration: connect with a code. For a computer running Frameleaf's Studio helper. Choose Get a connection code, name the computer, and enter the code, shown once, on that computer. It connects to this server by itself. Details Details is closed until you need it: AI helpers: addresses, access keys and limits edits each AI destination and its limits, and under This server's AI service and how each computer answered shows the full inventory. Studio helpers: connection codes, limits for each person and history manages Studio helpers. The inventory shows, for each worker: A worker shows as ready once a check confirms it, not just because it has an address. Further down, Library analysis routes lists each kind of library work and the worker it goes to; a kind with no route is shown as refused. Render workers lists Studio helpers by when they last checked in (they call the server, so there's no address to show), and Restoration runners on this server lists the server processes holding restoration jobs right now. The inventory refreshes every 30 seconds while the page is open. If a refresh fails, the last snapshot stays on screen with its age. Check what it can run checks that one worker now and contacts nothing else. Machine learning addresses Machine-learning endpoints, in the invent

articles.title: Workflows
articles.description: Simple "when this happens, do that" rules for new uploads, with a dry run before you turn them on.
articles.intro: Workflows take routine sorting off your hands. They're simple rules that run on your server: when something happens, check a condition, then do something. For example: when a photo or video is uploaded, if it's a video, add it to an album and tag it.

headings.title: Triggers
headings.text: A workflow starts when:

headings.title: Build a workflow
headings.text: The workflow designer offers the triggers, filters and actions your server has installed. Add the steps you want, in order.

headings.title: Turn on, share and remove
headings.text: Turn a workflow on or off at any time, or delete it. You can also do this from the Frameleaf apps. Export a workflow as a JSON file to keep it or move it to another server, and import one the same way. Passwords and other credentials are removed from exports. Once a workflow's steps have run on an item, that run stays marked as finished.

headings.title: Other ways to automate
headings.text: Smart albums gather photos that match a rule. AI descriptions and smart albums sort photos into Travel, Food, Pets and more. Nightly jobs, such as database backups and integrity checks, run on their own.

articles.title: Your Frameleaf account
articles.description: Link your server to Frameleaf, sign in with one account and invite your family.
articles.intro: Your Frameleaf account connects your server to Frameleaf Cloud. Link it once and you get one sign-in for you and your family, plus remote access, backup and the other services in your plan. Prefer to stay fully local? A local photo account works without linking.

headings.title: Sign in
headings.text: Sign in from the link on your server or at the Frameleaf account site. Add a second recovery method in your account settings so you can always get back in.

headings.title: Link a server
headings.text: You need to be an administrator of the photo server, and Cloud needs to be configured for your release or deployment.

headings.title: Sign in with Frameleaf on your server
headings.text: Each person links their own account from Your preferences → Frameleaf account. Everyone keeps a private library: linking a server doesn't give its owner access to other people's photos. Share albums, items or shared spaces when you want others to see them.

headings.title: Share a server with people
headings.text: Invite family and friends from the server's Sharing page on the account site. Choose their role, send the invitation, and they accept with their own Frameleaf account. To share photos with them, use the library's sharing controls.

headings.title: Keep the server identity safe
headings.text: Your server's identity is stored with the installation. Keep it, together with the Manager recovery configuration, in your private recovery plan. Run each linked identity on one server only.

headings.title: Licences, plans and credit
headings.text: Activate a supporter licence on the linked server before you buy a Cloud plan or AI credit. A licence is paid once and lasts for life.

headings.title: Unlink a server
headings.text: Unlink from Account & link on the server or from the server controls on the account site. Unlinking stops remote access, linked sign-in, new Cloud processing and scheduled Cloud backups.

headings.title: Close or delete your account
headings.text: To delete your Frameleaf account, or close it without erasing it, see Delete your account. Export any information and recover any backups you need first. Neither touches the files on your server.

articles.text: Your Frameleaf account connects your server to Frameleaf Cloud. Link it once and you get one sign-in for you and your family, plus remote access, backup and the other services in your plan. Prefer to stay fully local? A local photo account works without linking. You'll meet three accounts: the Manager administrator runs the installation, your local photo account lives on your server, and your Frameleaf account connects Cloud services. articles.title: Buddy backup
articles.description: Swap encrypted backups with a friend's Frameleaf server, so each of you has an off-site copy at no extra storage cost.
articles.intro: Buddy backup gives you an off-site copy of your library on a friend's Frameleaf server, and you host theirs in return. Each server keeps an encrypted backup of the other. Your Frameleaf account handles pairing, but your photos go straight between the two servers, and neither your buddy nor Frameleaf Cloud can read them.

headings.title: How does Buddy Backup work?
headings.text: Your server encrypts its backup, then sends it to your buddy's server. Your buddy stores the encrypted files but can't open them: only your own recovery kit unlocks your backup. The two directions have their own storage allowances, keys and restore points.

headings.title: What you need
headings.text: Both servers need a Server licence to start a new Buddy Backup pairing. A Frameleaf Cloud plan is needed only when the servers can't connect directly and use the relay.

headings.title: Set it up
headings.text: Open Settings, then Backup, then Buddy Backup. The Frameleaf Cloud, then Cloud backup entry opens the same backup area.

headings.title: What's protected
headings.text: Every user's originals, videos, Live Photo parts, sidecars, edits, project files and metadata, plus external libraries whose drives are connected when the backup runs. Each restore point also includes a verified database dump, Frameleaf settings, user preferences and the configuration files you declared during setup. It's not a whole operating-system image.

headings.title: Two directions
headings.text: My backup shows your latest complete restore point, and separately, your latest successful restore check. Hosting for my buddy shows the space used and reserved. It never shows their file names, albums or photos.

headings.title: Defaults
headings.text: Change the schedule, transfer windows and limits under Hosting & transfer settings. When either side runs out of agreed space or free disk, receiving pauses. Protected restore points are never deleted to make room.

headings.title: Restore
headings.text: Unlock with your PIN and choose a dated restore point. Restore a photo or video, a selection or an album; administrators can also restore a whole library, the settings or the entire server. The wizard previews what will change and any conflicts before it starts. By default it fills in what's missing and keeps your current changes; choosing to replace keeps a rollback copy. articles.title: Cloud backup
articles.description: Keep an encrypted, off-site copy of your library with 1 TB included in your Cloud plan, and restore it whenever you need to.
articles.intro: Cloud backup keeps an encrypted copy of your library away from your home, so a failed disk, fire or theft doesn't cost you your photos. Your Cloud plan includes 1 TB of Frameleaf-managed storage, or you can back up to a compatible storage bucket you manage yourself. It's in addition to Manager's database-only backup.

headings.title: Licence and plan
headings.text: Managed Cloud Backup needs both a live Cloud plan and a supporter licence activated on the linked server; neither works on its own. A Server licence covers every account on that server; an Individual licence covers only its owner's own account. On older server releases, new backups need a Server licence, so update your server before relying on Individual coverage. Your own storage bucket has its own setup.

headings.title: Turn it on
headings.text: Open Settings → Backup or Frameleaf Cloud → Backup, then start the Cloud backup setup.

headings.title: Choose how the key is kept
headings.text: You can let the server generate a key or supply one yourself. The setup screen explains how to recover with each option. If you choose not to save the key on the server, you enter it again when the server restarts or when you restore.

headings.title: What's backed up
headings.text: Coverage follows your activated licences, account by account; you don't choose individual albums, people or dates. The database copy always covers the whole library, even when only some accounts' originals are covered. Generated previews and transcoded media have their own options.

headings.title: Schedule, retention and checks
headings.text: Set the schedule and retention on your server. Keep enough restore points to recover from a mistake you only notice later, and keep an eye on free storage and the last successful run.

headings.title: Restore
headings.text: Choose the restore point and what to restore. Check the destination and any conflicts. Confirm.

headings.title: When your backup grows
headings.text: The standard web plan includes 1 TB. When you need more, storage grows automatically in started 1 TB blocks at $9.99 per block per month, including on an annual plan. Licence discounts don't apply to extra storage. Fixed-size plans bought through a mobile store have their own upgrade and plan-full controls.

headings.title: Read-only states
headings.text: If your last qualifying licence ends, new managed backup writes stop, but your existing backup data, keys and restores stay available and nothing is purged. Reinstate a qualifying licence and writes resume while your plan is live. Cancelling the plan has its own retention and deletion rules.

articles.title: Cloud GPU
articles.description: Run heavy AI jobs on fast Cloud GPUs, with a price estimate and your approval before anything starts.
articles.intro: Cloud GPU runs heavy jobs, such as descriptions, enhancement, restoration, captions and voice-overs, on fast remote hardware, so you get results quickly without buying a graphics card. You see what will be sent and what it will cost before each job starts, and you only pay for the work that's done.

headings.title: Before you start
headings.text: An administrator sets it up once:

headings.title: Choose what leaves your server
headings.text: Each Cloud job sends only the inputs that task needs, and the dialog shows you exactly what that is before you confirm. Different tools send different things: a description preview, restoration inputs, transcription audio or a voice-over script.

headings.title: Run a job
headings.text: Open the description, enhancement, restoration, caption or voice-over tool. Choose a model and the Cloud destination. Check what will be sent, the estimated cost and your spending limit. Confirm the job. Follow progress in Recent cloud jobs or Activity, then see the result in your library.

headings.title: How you pay
headings.text: When you confirm, the estimate is reserved in your AI Wallet, not spent. You're charged only for the work actually completed, up to the reserved amount and within the terms you accepted. The rest of the reservation comes back to your available balance, and a job with no billable usage releases all of it. Work that finished before a failed item or an interruption is still charged.

headings.title: Automatic descriptions
headings.text: Turn on Describe new photos automatically to have each new upload described in the Cloud without asking each time. It's a separate opt-in with its own budget and consent. Describing your existing photos is a separate backfill. Turn it off at any time to go back to approving each request yourself.

headings.title: Review the result
headings.text: AI descriptions can get things wrong, and restoration can invent detail. Check a few results before applying changes across a large collection. Your originals are always kept, and Library Care and backup verification keep protecting your library whatever you process.

articles.title: Delete your account
articles.description: Delete your Frameleaf account on the web or in the app, what's erased and kept, how to change your mind, and how to delete a photo account on a server.
articles.intro: You can delete your Frameleaf account yourself, on the web or in the Frameleaf app. You don't need the app installed to do it.

headings.title: Delete your Frameleaf account on the web
headings.text: Go to frameleaf.cloud/privacy/delete and sign in. Read What happens when you delete your account. Under Confirm deleting, type DELETE. Select Delete my account in 30 days. If Frameleaf asks you to confirm it's you, use your passkey or the sign-in code sent to your email.

headings.title: Delete your Frameleaf account in the app
headings.text: Open Settings, then Frameleaf Cloud account. Sign in if the app asks you to. Select Delete Account. Read what's erased and kept, then select Continue. Check the deletion date and select Yes, continue. Type DELETE, then confirm it's you with your passkey or a sign-in code.

headings.title: What happens next
headings.text: Nothing is deleted for 30 days. Until then your account works as before, except that you can't add funds to your AI Wallet and automatic top-up doesn't run.

headings.title: Change your mind
headings.text: You can cancel during the 30 days:

headings.title: Close your account instead
headings.text: Closing switches your account off without erasing it. Every server is unlinked, every device is signed out, your plan ends at the end of the billing period, and Cloud backups are kept read-only. Frameleaf support can reactivate a closed account.

headings.title: Can't sign in?
headings.text: Email support@frameleaf.app from the address on your account and ask for it to be deleted. We may ask you to prove the account is yours before we act.

headings.title: Delete a photo account on a server
headings.text: Your photo account belongs to the server you use, so the server's administrator deletes it. Ask them to delete it, and save any photos and videos you want to keep first.

It holds your plan, licences, linked servers and Cloud services. Deleting it is covered first on this page. headings.title: Turn it on
headings.text: Link the server from Settings → Frameleaf Cloud → Account & link. Open Remote access and check the plan notice. Enable remote access and wait for the connection and certificate status to show ready. Copy the server address or use its QR code. Try it from another network, such as your phone's mobile connection.

headings.title: Routes
headings.text: A direct connection depends on your router, firewall and internet provider, and uses port 2443 by default. If a direct connection can't be made, the relay gets you there instead. Some corporate firewalls, captive portals and network policies block outgoing connections.

headings.title: Your server's addresses
headings.text: Your server shows its addresses on this page. Public server URL sets the address used in shared links and emails, so test it from the networks people will use.

headings.title: Limits
headings.text: Your server and the account site show your current relay usage and plan limits. Direct and relay routes can have different speeds and download policies, so check them before downloading a large archive or full originals remotely.

headings.title: Who can sign in
headings.text: Remote routes use the linked sign-in your server allows. Public shared links are a separate way to share selected photos. API keys keep their owner's access and follow the remote-access policy.

headings.title: Privacy
headings.text: The relay carries encrypted traffic, and your server keeps its certificate's private key. To route connections, the service sees information such as addresses and the number of bytes transferred. What this server sends in the account-link settings shows the full details for your installation.

headings.title: If something stops
headings.text: Check local access first, then the Cloud link, licence, plan, connection and certificate status. Local browsing keeps working even while remote access is down. After changing DNS, router settings or your internet connection, test again from outside your network.

articles.text: Remote access lets you and your family reach your Frameleaf server and library away from home, from anywhere, just like a hosted photo service. Your phone keeps backing up while you're away, shared links work for everyone, and the Apple TV app connects through it. If you'd rather run it yourself, you can also use a VPN or your own reverse proxy. What you need With a linked server and a Server licence, your server gets its Frameleaf direct address and certificate on its own, with no plan. The relay, your own hostname through the relay and the Frameleaf apps away from home need a Frameleaf Cloud plan. Without a plan, Remote access, then Relay shows Needs a plan with See plans, and the connection mode stays on Relay and direct. If your plan ends but the licence stays active, the relay stops and the direct address keeps working. Turn it on Link the server from Settings → Frameleaf Cloud → Account & link. Open Remote access and check the plan notice. Enable remote access and wait for the connection and certificate status to show ready. Copy the server address or use its QR code. Try it from another network, such as your phone's mobile connection. If the page reports a problem, it tells you the reason so you can fix it. Your server's addresses Your server shows its addresses on this page. Public server URL sets the address used in shared links and emails, so test it from the networks people will use. Use your own hostname Put your library on your own domain, such as photos.example.com. A hostname through the relay needs a Cloud plan: Add a subdomain you control in Remote access. Copy the DNS records shown into your DNS provider's settings exactly. Wait for verification and the certificate to be ready. Test the hostname from another network, then share it. If verification fails, compare your DNS records with the requested values and check whether the domain restricts which certificate authorities may issue for it. Limits Your server and the account site show your current relay usage and plan limits. Direct and relay routes can have different speeds and download policies, so check them before downloading a large archive or full originals remotely. Originals over the relay Your administrator can limit large original, archive and database-backup downloads over the relay. If a download isn't offered, use a home or direct connection, or ask your administrator about the policy. Previews may still load over the relay when originals don't. Who can sign in Remote routes use the linked sign-in your server allows. Public shared links are a separate way to share selected photos. API keys keep their owner's access and follow the remote-access policy. Each person links their own Frameleaf account. See Your Frameleaf account and Sharing. Before you unlink or cancel, make sure you have a local administrator sign-in and another way to reach the server.

articles.title: Ask Frameleaf
articles.description: Get sourced answers from Frameleaf's documentation, find the right processing options for your hardware and prepare your installation privately.
articles.intro: Open Ask Frameleaf for quick, sourced help with setup, backups, privacy, features and GPU choices. Answers come from the same reviewed public documentation you can read on this website, with links back to each guide so you can read more.

headings.title: Prepare your installation
headings.text: Choose Set up Frameleaf for a checklist tailored to your platform. Frameleaf Manager is the recommended path for a new library or an import from Immich. The advanced manual Docker option walks you through storage, hardware and supported settings.

headings.title: Choose processing and models
headings.text: Ask What can my GPU run? and give the exact model, available memory, platform and runtime. Recommendations are conservative estimates, and shared system memory counts differently from dedicated GPU memory. Try a sample in Frameleaf before you process your whole library. See Choose processing for your hardware.

headings.title: What is sent when you ask
headings.text: Your question, a limited amount of the current conversation and relevant public help excerpts are sent to a hosted AI service. Ask can't see your account, server, photo library or jobs, so keep passwords, recovery keys, private photos and account details out of your questions.

headings.title: Check the sources
headings.text: Every answer links to its sources, so you can read the full guide before you change your installation. If Ask can't answer confidently, it asks for more detail or points you to useful guides. Your running server always shows the settings and models it actually supports.

articles.title: Choose processing for your hardware
articles.description: Match photo and video tasks to your CPU, GPU and memory, and add Cloud GPU for the heavy jobs.
articles.intro: You don't need a GPU to get started. Install with the CPU setup, try a small sample, and add hardware or Cloud processing as your library grows. The hardware guide explains device access and supported runtimes, and Ask Frameleaf can help you narrow your choices.

headings.title: Match the task to the hardware
headings.text: Machine learning and video transcoding have their own settings, and a GPU that handles video encoding well may still be too small for a description model. Smart search, faces and text recognition run on your server or a worker on your own network, and Studio's final export stays at home too. For heavier tasks, Cloud jobs are there when you want them, with a clear destination and a cost estimate before anything runs.

headings.title: Choose a description model
headings.text: The description model table lists supported model families with memory estimates, and the adviser adds working-memory headroom on top. Its local recommendations cover reviewed NVIDIA Ampere and Ada configurations using CUDA; for other hardware it points you to the right guide and asks for the details it needs.

headings.title: Compare a sample first
headings.text: Use Preview a description to try a small sample before you change the whole library. Changing a search model can mean rebuilding its embeddings. See Search models and AI descriptions.

headings.title: If a model fails to load
headings.text: Check the model family is supported, then check the runtime, download source and free memory. Read the machine learning logs. A failed download and an out-of-memory error need different fixes. Test one item before you retry a full queue.

articles.text: Quick answers to the questions people ask most, grouped by topic. Can't find yours? Try Troubleshooting, the release notes, or search and ask in GitHub Issues and GitHub Discussions. General Do I need Frameleaf Cloud? No. Your photo library runs fully on your own server without a Cloud subscription. Cloud adds remote access, managed backup and GPU services when you want them, each with its own licence, plan and consent. The Apple TV app is the one exception: it needs a Frameleaf account and remote-access entitlement, even on your home network. See Frameleaf Cloud and Apple TV. Can I view my library on Apple TV? Yes. The native Apple TV app browses albums, people, places and memories and plays slideshows. Sign in using the QR code or short code shown on the TV. It needs tvOS 26 or later and an eligible server linked to your Frameleaf account. See the Apple TV guide for controls and settings. How do I install the Synology SPK? Install it from Package Center → Manual Install: Download the approved package and checksum from the Synology guide, and verify the checksum. In DSM, choose Package Center → Manual Install and select the package. Open Manager from the DSM main menu, at the same HTTPS address as DSM. Native DSM setup needs no external Manager port and no claim key. Where are my photos stored? On your server, as ordinary files in the folder you set as UPLOAD_LOCATION. Frameleaf adds thumbnails and video previews alongside them. Your albums, people and descriptions are in the database, in DB_DATA_LOCATION. Is Frameleaf open source? Yes. The Frameleaf Library community edition is open source under AGPLv3 at github.com/Frameleaf/frameleaf-app. Will Frameleaf save me money? Probably not. There are no monthly fees to run Frameleaf on your own server, but there are other costs: hardware, disks, storage for backups and your own time. There are many good reasons to host your own photos; saving money is rarely one of them. Can I bring a library from another photo application? Yes. Use a supported import or an export of your originals; start with Bring an existing library. A database import creates a fresh Frameleaf database of its own. Can I switch from Immich? Is Frameleaf still backward compatible? Yes, you can switch with a one-time import. Support for Immich backward compatibility ends on October 15, 2026. Switch from Immich uses Frameleaf Manager to import a supported source into a fresh Frameleaf database, with your media staying right where it is. The new Frameleaf system uses PostgreSQL 19 and database-backed job queues, with no Redis to run. The import is a one-time move for supported sources, so plan to settle on Frameleaf: the two applications don't share a database or switch back and forth. Can I pay for a particular feature to be built? No. There's no feature sponsorship or bounty scheme, and development priorities aren't for sale. You can suggest features in GitHub Discussions. Accounts and sign-in How do I reset the admin password? Run this on the server and follow the prompts: See Server commands for the other commands. How do I see every user on the server? Administrators can also see everyone in Settings, then Users. Do I need a setup code for a new server? No. A new server has no setup code. Anyone on its home network can set it up until it has an administrator, so set it up soon after installing. See First steps. How do I change my profile picture? Open a photo, choose the three-dot menu in the top right, then Set as profile picture. Zoom with the scroll wheel until the photo fills the circle, drag it into position and choose Save. Phone apps Which phones are supported? Frameleaf has native apps for iPhone and iPad (iOS 26 or later) and Android (Android 11 or later). Install from the App Store or Google Play, or use the web app in your phone's browser. See iPhone and Android apps. articles.title: Supported formats
articles.description: The photo, RAW and video file types Frameleaf accepts.
articles.intro: Bring photos and videos from your phone, your camera and other apps. Frameleaf accepts every format below, including RAW files from all the major camera makers. Your originals are always stored exactly as uploaded, and Frameleaf makes thumbnails, previews and a video copy that plays smoothly in browsers and on phones.

headings.title: RAW files
headings.text: Enhanced RAW rendering

headings.title: Live Photos and Motion Photos
headings.text: Apple Live Photos (a still photo and a short .mov) and Android Motion Photos are kept together as one item that plays its motion. If the two halves of a Live Photo were uploaded separately, rejoin them with Utilities, then Live Photo pairing. See Library Care.

headings.title: Sidecar files
headings.text: Frameleaf reads and writes .xmp sidecar files next to your originals. Changes you make to dates, locations, descriptions, ratings and tags are saved there, and existing sidecars from other apps are read when a file is imported.

headings.title: Something isn't accepted?
headings.text: Files with an extension that isn't listed are rejected on upload and skipped in external libraries. Convert the file to a supported format first, or suggest the format in GitHub Discussions if you think it should be supported.

Photos RAW files Enhanced RAW rendering Some RAW files, older Canon .cr2 files for example, have a missing or unusable embedded preview. With Enhanced RAW rendering on, Frameleaf uses the embedded preview first and falls back to a full render with LibRaw when it needs to, so these files still get proper thumbnails and previews. It's on by default, in Settings, then Editing & playback, then Image previews. A RAW file that can't be rendered is reported as unsupported, separately from files that are actually damaged. See Library Care. When you review duplicates, Frameleaf suggests keeping a RAW original over a JPEG copy, and HEIC or HEIF over JPEG, even when the JPEG is bigger. headings.title: Running on Windows
headings.text: Frameleaf runs best with Docker on Linux, so use that if you can. On Windows, run Docker through WSL 2, and keep the database on a Linux filesystem or a Docker volume, never on an NTFS folder. See Requirements.

headings.title: Start again from scratch
headings.text: If a test installation is beyond repair, see How do I wipe Frameleaf and start again?. This deletes everything, so keep it for test installations only.

articles.text: Most problems have a quick fix, and this page walks you through the common ones. The logs almost always point the way. If you installed with Manager, start with Overview → Logs and the error recorded for the operation. Keep the Manager state and database folders in place while you work out what went wrong. Still stuck? Read the release notes for known issues, then search or ask in GitHub Issues and GitHub Discussions. Include your Frameleaf version, how you installed it and the relevant lines from the logs, so people can help you faster. Useful Docker commands See the containers From the folder with your docker-compose.yml, you can also use: Read the logs Add --follow to keep streaming new lines while you reproduce a problem. If your containers have different names, use the ones docker ps shows: To make the server log more, set FRAMELEAF_LOG_LEVEL in .env. See Environment variables and Monitoring. Open a shell in a container Run server commands See Server commands. Installation problems docker compose fails with "unknown shorthand flag: 'd'" or "permission denied" Run docker compose version to check you have Compose v2. An unknown shorthand flag error usually means an old or incompatible Docker package. An .env: permission denied error means the user running Compose can't read that file, so check its permissions. To get a current version, follow Docker's Engine install guide for your distribution, including Uninstall old versions and Install using the apt repository (or rpm), to replace it with Docker's own packages. "'name' does not match any of the regexes: '^x-'" You ran docker-compose (with a hyphen), which is deprecated and isn't supported. Use docker compose from a current Docker install. "can't set healthcheck.start_interval" The full message is can't set healthcheck.start_interval as feature require Docker Engine v25 or later. Update to Docker Engine v25 or later, and keep the health checks in place: they tell you when a container fails to start. See Unraid. I can't open the web app Check the required containers are running with docker compose ps. If one keeps restarting, read its logs. Open http:// :2283, using the server's address on your network, not localhost, from another device. On Synology, check the firewall and HTTPS settings. The native app uses the configured DSM HTTPS origin and port, normally 5001, through /frameleaf-manager/. Its Manager listener on 9443 stays local to the NAS. Your photo library uses its separate application port, normally 2283. Inspect server and database logs in Frameleaf Manager → Services → View log. If you use a reverse proxy, try the direct address first to rule it out. See Reverse proxy. A new server can't be set up A new server can only be set up from its home network. Open the web app, or use the Frameleaf app, from a device on the same network, not through remote access or a proxy on the internet. For a server that isn't at home, see Setting up a new server remotely. Setup ends once the server has an administrator. If someone has already set it up, sign in with that account. If the server is already linked to a Frameleaf account, the apps join it with Sign in with Frameleaf instead of setting it up. Database problems The database container keeps restarting Read its log with docker logs frameleaf_postgres. The usual causes: `data directory ... has wrong ownership`: the database folder is on a filesystem without Unix ownership and permissions, such as NTFS or exFAT, or on a folder mounted from Windows into WSL. Move DB_DATA_LOCATION to a supported filesystem or a Docker volume. See Requirements. Permission denied: the folder isn't writable. On Unraid, this happens when DB_DATA_LOCATION is left at its default; see Unraid. On TrueNAS, check dataset permissions against the user used by the release's database image; see TrueNAS. A network share: the database must be on local storage. Network shares aren't supported. Check the database for corruption New installations have database ch
